sections.title: Names, Values, and =
sections.body:
A **variable** is a name that points at a value. You make one with `=`, which is not the equals of mathematics: it means store the value on the right under the name on the left.

Python evaluates the right-hand side first and only then binds the name, which is why `score = score + 10` is sensible rather than circular - it reads the old value, adds, and stores the result back under the same name.

`print()` shows values. Hand it several values separated by commas and it prints them on one line with a single space between them.
sections.code:
score = 42
print(score)

score = score + 10
print(score)

name = "Mira"
print(name, "has", score, "points")

annotations.text: The name score now points at the integer 42. Nothing is printed yet - assignment is silent.
The right side is computed with the old value (42 + 10), then 52 is stored back under score.
Four values, one print, one line. Each comma inserts a single space - you do not add them yourself.

checkpoint.prompt: Store the number 100 in a variable called `score`, then add 25 to it, then print the result. The program must print exactly `125`.
checkpoint.starterCode:
# store 100 in score

# add 25 to it

# print it
checkpoint.explain: Assignment stores and print shows - two separate acts, which is why a program that only computes appears to do nothing at all. Reading `score` on the right of `score = score + 25` uses the value bound a moment earlier, then rebinds the same name.

sections.title: Four Kinds of Value
sections.body:
Every value has a **type**, and the type decides what that value is allowed to do. Four of them carry this whole floor: `int` for whole numbers, `float` for numbers with a decimal point, `str` for text inside quotes, and `bool` for exactly `True` and `False`.

`type(x)` reports which one you are holding, and it is the first thing worth checking when Python complains about a line that looks obviously fine.

Note that `7` and `7.0` are equal in value but different in type, and `"7"` is not a number at all - it is text that merely looks like one.
sections.code:
level = 7
ratio = 0.5
name = "Mira"
ready = True

print(level, ratio, name, ready)
print(type(level), type(ratio))
print(type(name), type(ready))

annotations.text: True and False are capitalised and take no quotes. "True" with quotes would be a str instead.
type() hands back the type object itself, which prints as <class 'int'>.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print? Write all four lines.
checkpoint.explain: A single decimal point turns an int into a float, and a pair of quotes turns either one into text. Recognising these four names on sight is what makes Python's error messages readable later, since they name types rather than values.

sections.title: Operators Do Different Work
sections.body:
An **operator** does different work depending on the types either side of it. On numbers, `+`, `-` and `*` behave as you expect, while `/` always produces a `float`, `//` divides and throws the remainder away, `%` keeps only that remainder, and `**` raises to a power.

On text, `+` joins two strings end to end and `*` repeats one a whole number of times.

Mixing the two is where every beginner gets stuck: `"Level " + 7` raises a `TypeError`, because Python refuses to guess whether you meant text or arithmetic.
sections.code:
print(7 + 2, 7 - 2, 7 * 2)
print(7 / 2, 7 // 2, 7 % 2)
print(2 ** 10)
print("ha" * 3, "sun" + "flower")

annotations.text: / gives 3.5 even though 7 and 2 are both ints; // gives the whole part and % the leftover.
The same two symbols applied to text: * repeats and + joins. Neither one adds anything.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print? Write all three lines.
checkpoint.explain: `//` and `%` are the two halves of one division: 10 is three lots of 3 with 1 left over, and together they lose nothing. Repetition on a string produces a longer string rather than a number, which is why the last line adds nothing up.

sections.title: Showing and Reading
sections.body:
An **f-string** is a string with an `f` before its opening quote: whatever you write inside `{}` is evaluated and pasted in as text, so `f"Level {level}"` needs no `+` and no conversion of its own.

`input()` reads one line typed by the user and always hands back a `str`, even when what was typed looks like a number. `int()`, `float()` and `str()` convert between types: `int("7") + 1` is `8`, while `"7" + 1` is a `TypeError`.

Convert the moment you read, and the rest of the program never has to think about it again.
sections.code:
raw = "7"
print(raw + raw)
print(int(raw) + int(raw))

level = int(raw)
print(f"Level {level} of 10, {level * 10}% done")

annotations.text: Pretend this line is raw = input() and the user typed 7. Either way, raw holds text.
Two strings joined gives 77, not 14. This is the bug hiding inside almost every first program.
Inside {} you may put any expression, so level * 10 is computed first and pasted in as text.

checkpoint.prompt: Fill the blanks so that typing `4` prints `Level 4, next is 5`.
checkpoint.template:
raw = input()
level = ___(raw)
print(f"Level {level}, next is {level ___ 1}")
checkpoint.explain: The conversion has to happen before the arithmetic, because `"4" + 1` means nothing to Python. Once level is an int, the braces can hold a whole expression rather than only a bare name.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print? Write all three lines.
guided-practice.code:
gold = 3
print(gold)
gold = gold * 4
print(gold)
gold = gold - 2
print(gold)
guided-practice.explain: Each line rebinds the same name using whatever it holds at that moment, so the program must be read top to bottom rather than as a set of equations. If these were equations, `gold = gold * 4` would have no solution at all.
guided-practice.hint: Work out the right-hand side first, then write down the new value of gold.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print? Write all three lines.
guided-practice.explain: Commas inside one print produce one line with single spaces between the values, which is why the first line is not two lines. The middle line shows `/` reaching for a float even when both operands are ints, while `//` and `%` stay in whole numbers.
guided-practice.hint: Two values in one print land on the same line.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the blanks so this prints `7` on the first line and `7.0` on the second.
guided-practice.explain: Both conversions read the same text and neither one changes `raw` - each builds a brand new value of a different type. The trailing `.0` is Python reporting that the second value is a float, not that it is somehow more precise.
guided-practice.hint: One converter gives whole numbers, the other keeps a decimal point.

guided-practice.prompt: Give the value of `gold` after each of the last three lines runs.
guided-practice.code:
gold = 10
gold = gold + 5
gold = gold * 2
gold = gold - 30
guided-practice.explain: Only one value exists at a time and each line replaces it, so the order of the lines is the whole meaning of the program. Writing the running value beside each line is the cheapest debugging technique there is, and it scales to programs far larger than this one.
guided-practice.hint: Carry the number from the previous line into the next.

guided-practice.prompt: Order these lines into a program that reads a number of coins, adds 5, and reports the new total.
guided-practice.explain: Every line needs the name that the line above it created, so the data dependencies fix the order completely. Python runs top to bottom and has no way to use a name before the statement that binds it has run.
guided-practice.hint: Nothing can be converted before it has been read.

guided-practice.prompt: Write a program that reads one line - a name - and prints exactly `Hello, <name>!` using an f-string. For the input `Mira` it must print `Hello, Mira!`.
guided-practice.starterCode:
name = input()
# print the greeting with an f-string
guided-practice.solution:
name = input()
print(f"Hello, {name}!")
guided-practice.explain: `input()` takes the entire line, spaces included, which is why a two-word name arrives intact instead of as two values. The f-string keeps the literal text and the variable in one readable piece rather than splitting the sentence across `+` joins.
guided-practice.hint1: input() gives you the whole line as a string.
guided-practice.hint2: An f-string starts with f before the quote: f"...".

guided-practice.prompt: This program should read a number of years and print the number one year later, but it crashes with a `TypeError`. Fix it. For the input `10` it must print `11`.
guided-practice.starterCode:
years = input()
print(years + 1)
guided-practice.solution:
years = int(input())
print(years + 1)
guided-practice.explain: The fault is not in the arithmetic but in what `input()` returned: text. Converting at the point of reading fixes every later line at once, whereas converting inside the print would leave the same trap waiting for the next line you add.
guided-practice.hint1: What type does input() always return?
guided-practice.hint2: You cannot add 1 to a piece of text.

guided-practice.prompt: Write a program that reads two whole numbers, `a` then `b`, one per line, and prints three lines: `a + b`, then `a - b`, then `a * b`. For the input `6` then `3` it must print `9`, then `3`, then `18`.
guided-practice.starterCode:
a = int(input())
b = int(input())
# print the three results, one per line
guided-practice.solution:
a = int(input())
b = int(input())
print(a + b)
print(a - b)
print(a * b)
guided-practice.explain: Two calls to `input()` consume two separate lines in the order they were typed, so the read for `b` must come after the read for `a`. Keeping each result in its own `print` is what puts them on three lines - commas would have collapsed all three onto one.
guided-practice.hint1: Call input() twice, converting each time.
guided-practice.hint2: Subtraction is not symmetric: the prompt asks for a - b.
guided-practice.hint3: Three separate print calls give three separate lines.

exam.prompt: A program runs `age = input()` and the user types `30`. What is now stored in `age`?
choices: nothing, until the value is converted
exam.explain: Reading never inspects what was typed - `input()` hands back the line as text and stops there. That single fact accounts for almost every TypeError a first program produces.

exam.prompt: What does this program print? Write all three lines.
exam.code:
tag = "ha"
print(tag * 3)
print(tag + tag + "!")
print("-" * 5)
exam.explain: `*` on a string means repeat and `+` means join, so neither one produces a number however numeric the operands look. Repeating a single character is the standard way to draw a rule across the screen without typing it out.

exam.prompt: Fill the blanks so this prints `Mira has 12 gold`.
exam.explain: Without the prefix the braces are just characters and the line prints them literally - that one letter is what switches substitution on. Inside the braces you name the variable itself, never the text you are hoping to see.
exam.hint: One blank is a single letter in front of the quote.

exam.prompt: Which of these expressions produce a value of type `str`?
exam.explain: Conversion, joining, f-string substitution and reading a line all end in text; only the bare arithmetic stays numeric. Noticing that `input()` belongs in this group is exactly what stops you adding 1 to a line the user typed.

exam.prompt: Order these lines into a program that reads a weight in grams and prints it in kilograms, for example `1.5 kg`.
exam.explain: Each name is created exactly one line before it is used, so only one order runs at all. Building the text into a variable before printing it is a habit worth keeping: it separates deciding what to say from saying it.
exam.hint: Find the only line that uses no earlier name - that one goes first.

exam.prompt: A player types `7` into this program and expects to see `12`, but it prints `75`. Explain in your own words what is actually happening and what you would change.
exam.code:
coins = input()
bonus = "5"
print(coins + bonus)
exam.explain: Nothing here crashes, which is what makes it dangerous: both operands are strings, so `+` did exactly what it promises for text and joined them. A bug that produces a plausible-looking answer calls for the types to be checked, not the arithmetic.
exam.hint: Look at the type of the value on each side of the +.

exam.prompt: Trace `value` through this program. Write each state exactly as Python would show it: text in single quotes, numbers bare.
exam.code:
value = "6"
value = value + "6"
value = int(value)
value = value // 5
exam.explain: One name carries a different type at different moments, so `+` joins on the second line and `//` divides two lines later. Tracking the type alongside the value - not just the digits - is what tells you which meaning of an operator is about to apply.
exam.hint1: The first two lines are string work, not arithmetic.
exam.hint2: int("66") is the moment the type changes.
exam.hint3: // keeps only the whole part of the division.

exam.prompt: What does this program print? Write all three lines.
exam.code:
total = 7
people = 2
print(f"{total} split {people} ways")
print(f"each gets {total / people}")
print(f"whole units: {total // people}")
exam.answer:
7 split 2 ways
each gets 3.5
whole units: 3
exam.explain: Braces hold expressions, not only names, so each division runs before anything is printed and its result is pasted in as text. The last two lines differ by one character and by an entire type: one produces 3.5, the other 3.

exam.prompt: This should read a total number of items, then how many fit in one box, and print `Boxes filled: N` counting only completely filled boxes. It crashes instead. Fix it. For the input `7` then `2` it must print `Boxes filled: 3`.
exam.starterCode:
total = int(input())
per_box = int(input())
print("Boxes filled: " + total / per_box)
exam.solution:
total = int(input())
per_box = int(input())
print(f"Boxes filled: {total // per_box}")
exam.explain: Two faults sit on one line: text cannot be joined to a number, and `/` would have reported half a box even once the join was repaired. The word 'completely' in a specification is almost always the signal to reach for `//` rather than `/`.
exam.hint1: A partly filled box does not count.
exam.hint3: An f-string removes the need to join text to a number at all.

exam.prompt: Write a shop receipt program. It reads three lines: an item name, the price of one item as a whole number of coins, then the quantity as a whole number. It prints exactly two lines - first `<quantity> x <name>`, then `Total: <price times quantity> coins`. For the input `potion`, `5`, `3` it prints `3 x potion` and then `Total: 15 coins`.
exam.starterCode:
name = input()
price = int(input())
quantity = int(input())
# print the two lines
exam.solution:
name = input()
price = int(input())
quantity = int(input())
print(f"{quantity} x {name}")
print(f"Total: {price * quantity} coins")
exam.explain: Every idea on this floor meets here: three reads in a fixed order, two conversions, one multiplication, and two f-strings mixing stored values with literal text. The zero cases need no special handling - multiplying by zero and printing the result falls out of the same code, which is what a well-shaped program should do.
exam.hint1: Read all three lines first, in the order the prompt lists them.
exam.hint2: Only the last two reads need int().
exam.hint3: Two f-strings, two print calls, and the multiplication goes inside the braces.

sections.title: Asking Questions
sections.body:
A **comparison** asks a question about two values and answers it with a `bool` - either `True` or `False`. Python gives you six of them: `==` and `!=` for equality, and `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` for ordering.

The pair that catches everybody is `=` against `==`. A single `=` **stores** a value under a name and asks nothing at all; a doubled `==` **compares** two values and hands back an answer. Python refuses `=` inside a condition, which turns a whole family of silent bugs into a loud syntax error you cannot miss.
sections.code:
score = 60

print(score == 60)
print(score != 60)
print(score < 100, score > 100)
print(score <= 60, score >= 61)

annotations.text: A single = stores 60 under the name score. Nothing is compared here.
== compares and produces a bool, which print then shows you.
<= includes the boundary, >= on 61 does not - 60 is not 61 or more.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this program print?
checkpoint.code:
a = 4
b = 5
print(a == b)
print(a < b)
checkpoint.explain: Each comparison is evaluated into a single bool before print ever sees it, which is why the output is two words rather than the expressions themselves.

sections.title: Choosing a Branch
sections.body:
An `if` statement runs its indented block only when the condition is true. Adding `elif` branches offers alternatives, and a closing `else` catches everything left over.

Python tests the conditions **top to bottom and stops at the first true one** - the branches below it are never even evaluated, however true they might be. Because the body of an `if` is ordinary code, an `if` can sit inside another one, and the indentation is the only thing telling you which `else` belongs to which `if`.

annotations.text: 31 > 30 is true, so this branch runs and both branches below it are skipped.
A nested if: it is only reached because the outer condition was true.
This else belongs to the inner if - it means over 30 but not over 40.

checkpoint.prompt: Fill the blanks so that exactly one label prints, whatever the hour is.
checkpoint.template:
hour = 9
if hour < 12:
    print('morning')
___ hour < 18:
    print('afternoon')
___:
    print('evening')
checkpoint.explain: Chaining with elif is what makes the branches mutually exclusive. Three separate if statements would test all three conditions and could print two labels for one hour.

sections.title: Combining Conditions
sections.body:
Conditions join together with three words. `and` is true only when **both** sides are true, `or` is true when **at least one** side is, and `not` flips whatever follows it.

- `not` binds tightest, then `and`, then `or`
- brackets override that order, and are worth adding whenever the reading is not instant

Python also **short-circuits**: if the left side of an `and` is already false, the right side is never evaluated, because nothing it could say would change the answer.
sections.code:
age = 20
has_ticket = False

print(age >= 18 and has_ticket)
print(age >= 18 or has_ticket)
print(not has_ticket)
print(age >= 18 and not has_ticket)

annotations.text: The left side is true but the right is false, so and gives False.
or only needs one true side, so this is True.
not binds tighter than and, so this reads as (age >= 18) and (not has_ticket).

checkpoint.prompt: What does this program print?
checkpoint.code:
x = 5
print(x > 0 and x < 10)
print(x < 0 or x > 100)
print(not x == 5)
checkpoint.explain: Comparisons are resolved before the connecting word is applied, so the last line flips the result of x == 5 rather than comparing not x against 5.

sections.title: Truthy and Falsy
sections.body:
Any value at all can be used as a condition, not only a `bool`. Python treats the empty and zero ones as **falsy** - `0`, `0.0`, `""`, `[]`, `{}`, `None` and `False` - and absolutely everything else as **truthy**.

That is why `if items:` is the idiomatic way to ask whether a collection holds anything. One surprise travels with it: `and` and `or` hand back **one of their operands** rather than a `bool`, so `name or "anonymous"` gives you the name when there is one and the fallback when the name is empty.
sections.code:
print(bool(0), bool(""), bool([]), bool({}))
print(bool(3), bool("no"), bool([0]))

name = ""
print(name or "anonymous")

if not name:
    print("no name given")

annotations.text: Zero, the empty string, the empty list and the empty dict are all falsy.
A list holding a single zero is still non-empty, so it is truthy.
or returns the first truthy operand - the fallback string, since name is empty.
not turns the falsy empty string into True, so the message prints.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `is_blank(text)` returning `True` when `text` is the empty string and `False` otherwise. Test the string's own truthiness rather than comparing it to two quote marks.
checkpoint.explain: `not text` reads as 'there is no text' and already produces a bool, so no if statement is needed. A single space is a real character, which is why the third case comes out False.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print?
guided-practice.explain: A comparison is an expression like any other: it is evaluated down to a single bool before anything else happens to it. That is why you can print one, store it in a variable, or hand it straight to an if.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print?
guided-practice.explain: Only one branch of a chain can ever run. Python stops at the first true condition, so `x > 0` is never tested even though it would also have been true - which is exactly why the order of the branches is part of the logic.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the blanks so `grade(score)` returns 'pass' for 60 and above, and 'fail' for anything lower.
guided-practice.explain: The words '60 and above' include 60 itself, which is the whole difference between `>` and `>=`. Boundary bugs almost always come down to that one character rather than to the shape of the code.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `sign(n)` returning `1` when `n` is positive, `-1` when `n` is negative, and `0` when `n` is exactly zero.
guided-practice.starterCode:
def sign(n):
    pass
guided-practice.explain: Zero is neither positive nor negative, so three outcomes need three branches - a plain if/else would silently file zero under one of the other two. Falling off the end of the chain is itself a meaningful answer here.
guided-practice.hint: Three possible answers means the chain needs a third path.

guided-practice.prompt: Put these fragments in the order that defines `label(t)` so it returns 'freezing' below 0, 'mild' below 20, and 'hot' otherwise.
guided-practice.explain: Each branch's body is indented one level under its condition, and the chain has to run coldest first: a wider test placed earlier would swallow every narrower one below it. The final line needs no else, because a return has already left the function on every other path.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print?
guided-practice.code:
a = True
b = False
print(a and b)
print(a or b)
print(not a)
print(not (a and b))
guided-practice.explain: `and` demands both sides, `or` settles for one, and `not` flips whatever it is handed. The last line hands it a whole bracketed expression rather than a single name, so what gets flipped is the result of `a and b`.

guided-practice.prompt: This function will not even run - Python reports a syntax error on the `if` line. Fix it so `is_zero(n)` returns `True` only when `n` is zero.
guided-practice.explain: `=` stores a value and produces nothing to test, so Python rejects it in a condition outright. The rejection is a gift: in languages that permit it, this typo becomes a bug that runs happily and quietly does the wrong thing.
guided-practice.hint: One of these operators stores a value; the other asks a question.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `can_enter(age, has_ticket)` returning `True` only when `age` is at least 18 **and** `has_ticket` is true, and `False` otherwise.
guided-practice.starterCode:
def can_enter(age, has_ticket):
    pass
guided-practice.solution:
def can_enter(age, has_ticket):
    return age >= 18 and has_ticket
guided-practice.explain: The combined expression already is the answer, so returning it beats an if that returns True in one branch and False in the other. The 18 case is the one that matters: 'at least' means the boundary counts, so `>` would quietly turn away someone who qualifies.
guided-practice.hint: You can return the whole condition in one line.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print?
guided-practice.explain: Emptiness decides falsiness, not what a value contains. The string "0" is one character long and the list `[0]` holds one item, so both are truthy however zero-like they look - only the genuinely empty cases flip to False.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `greet(name)` returning `'Hello, ' + name`, except that when `name` is an empty string it returns `'Hello, stranger'`. Test the string's truthiness rather than comparing it to an empty string literal.
guided-practice.starterCode:
def greet(name):
    pass
guided-practice.explain: `if not name` reads as 'if there is no name' and handles the empty case without a second comparison. Dealing with the exceptional case first and returning early also keeps the ordinary path unindented, which is how most Python guard clauses are written.
guided-practice.hint: An empty string is falsy, so `not name` is already the test you need.

exam.prompt: Which line **asks** whether `x` currently holds 3, rather than making it hold 3?
exam.explain: One repeated character separates storing from asking. Python defends you inside a condition by refusing the single `=`, but on a line of its own each form is legal and only one of them is a question.

exam.prompt: Which of these values are **falsy** - that is, `bool(value)` is `False`?
exam.explain: Falsiness means empty or zero, nothing more. `'0'` is a string with a character in it and `-1` is a number that is not zero, so both count as true in a condition however small or negative they look.

exam.prompt: What does this program print?
exam.explain: The inner if is only reached because the outer one was true, so the else beside it means 'over 100 but not a member' rather than 'not over 100'. Indentation is the only signal of which else answers which if.

exam.prompt: Fill the blanks so `in_range(n)` is True only for values from 1 to 9 inclusive, and `outside(n)` is its exact opposite.
exam.explain: Both bounds have to hold at once, which is `and`; the opposite of a whole condition is `not` wrapped around it. Flipping each half separately is the classic mistake - the true opposite of 'at least 1 and at most 9' is 'below 1 **or** above 9'.

exam.prompt: With `x = 0` and `y = 4`, evaluate `not x and y > 3` one piece at a time. Give the value at each step.
exam.code:
x = 0
y = 4
result = not x and y > 3
exam.explain: `not` binds tighter than `and`, so the expression is really `(not x) and (y > 3)`. Applying `not` to a plain number sends it through truthiness first, which is how a zero ends up producing True.

exam.prompt: A login check is written `if username and password:`. A user types a name but leaves the password box blank, so `password` is the empty string. Explain what the condition evaluates to and why, and say whether `password` is ever compared against anything.
exam.explain: An empty string is falsy, so `and` finds a false operand and the whole condition is False without a single `==` being written or run. The value is judged on its own emptiness, which is what lets this one-line idiom reject a blank field for free.

exam.prompt: Write `letter_grade(score)` returning 'A' for 90 and above, 'B' for 80 to 89, 'C' for 70 to 79, and 'F' for anything below 70.
exam.starterCode:
def letter_grade(score):
    pass
exam.explain: Ordering the chain from the highest bound downwards means each elif already knows the earlier tests failed, so you never have to write `score >= 80 and score < 90`. Reverse the order and every passing score would come out as the loosest grade that matched it.
exam.hint: Start with the highest band and let each elif inherit what the tests above it ruled out.

exam.prompt: `band(150)` should be 'huge' but returns 'positive' instead - one branch can never run at all. Fix it so 'huge' is returned above 100, 'positive' for 1 to 100, and 'non-positive' for zero and below.
exam.explain: Every number over 100 is also over 0, so the wider test placed first consumes the narrower one and leaves it as dead code. In an if/elif chain the more specific condition has to come first, because only the first true branch ever runs.
exam.hint: Ask which of the two conditions is true for more values, then put the other one first.

exam.prompt: What does this program print?
exam.code:
name = ""
print(name or "anonymous")
print(0 or 5)
print(1 and 0)
print(bool(name))
exam.explain: `or` hands back the first truthy operand and `and` the first falsy one - they return an operand, not a bool, and only the last line forces one. That is what makes `name or "anonymous"` a default-value idiom rather than a comparison.

exam.prompt: A reactor is balanced in criticality when **all three** hold: the temperature is below 800, the neutrons emitted per second are above 500, and temperature times neutrons is below 500000. Write `is_criticality_balanced(temperature, neutrons_emitted)` returning `True` when it is balanced and `False` when it is not.
exam.starterCode:
def is_criticality_balanced(temperature, neutrons_emitted):
    pass
exam.explain: Chained `and`s read as a checklist where every item has to pass, and the two boundary cases show why the strict operators were the right choice: 800 exactly is not below 800, and 500 exactly is not above 500. Short-circuiting also means the multiplication is skipped entirely once an earlier check has failed.
exam.hint: Three conditions joined by and, returned directly.

exam.prompt: Write `ticket_price(age, is_member)`. Anyone under 5 gets in free and pays `0`. Anyone aged 65 or over pays `5`, member or not - so a 70-year-old member pays `5`, not `8`. Any other member pays `8`, and everybody else pays `12`.
exam.starterCode:
def ticket_price(age, is_member):
    pass
exam.explain: Writing each rule as its own early return makes the order of the branches the priority order, so no condition has to repeat what an earlier one already ruled out - the membership test never needs to add 'and not a pensioner'. `if is_member` is a truthiness test on a bool, so `== True` would add characters and nothing else.

lesson.title: Runes You Can Read, Spells You Can Name

sections.title: A String Is a Sequence
sections.body:
A **string** is a sequence of characters, and every character sits at a numbered position called an **index**. Counting starts at `0` from the left, and negative numbers count from the right, so `s[-1]` is always the last character.

A **slice** `s[a:b]` builds a new string from index `a` up to but not including `b`; leave a side empty to mean "from the start" or "to the end". `len(s)` gives you how many characters there are, so the last valid index is always `len(s) - 1`.

One asymmetry is worth memorising now: indexing past the end raises an `IndexError`, but slicing past the end simply gives you whatever it can - which is why `s[-1:]` is safe even when `s` is empty.
sections.code:
spell = "fireball"
print(spell[0])
print(spell[-1])
print(spell[0:4])
print(spell[4:])
print(len(spell))
print(spell[100:200] == "")

annotations.text: -1 is the last character; you never have to compute len(spell) - 1.
Stops before index 4, so this is 'fire' - four characters, not five.
An empty end means 'run to the end of the string'.
A slice that is entirely out of range returns '' instead of raising.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.explain: Index 1 is the second character because counting starts at zero, and -3 counts back from the end without needing len(). The slice stops before index 5, so it yields three characters, not four.

sections.title: Methods Hand Back New Strings
sections.body:
Strings are **immutable**: nothing can change the characters inside an existing string. So `upper()`, `lower()`, `strip()` and `replace(old, new)` never edit in place - each one builds and returns a **new** string and leaves the original exactly as it was.

That is why a method call on its own line accomplishes nothing: the new string is created and immediately thrown away. You must store the result, return it, or print it.

You can also interrogate a string. `"fire" in spell` is a `bool` saying whether that substring appears anywhere, and `spell.find("ball")` gives the index where it starts - or `-1` when it is absent, rather than an error.
sections.code:
name = "  Mira  "
print(name.strip().upper())
print(name)
print("mira".replace("i", "y"))
print("fire" in "fireball")
print("fireball".find("ball"))
print("fireball".find("ice"))

annotations.text: Methods chain left to right: strip() first, then upper() on its result.
The original still has its spaces and its lowercase letters. Nothing was modified.
find returns -1 for 'not here' - it never raises, so you must check for it.

checkpoint.prompt: Fill the blanks so this prints `HELLO` with no surrounding spaces.
checkpoint.explain: Each call is applied to the string the previous one returned, so the order in the chain is the order the work happens in. Reversing them would still work here, but only because uppercasing leaves spaces alone.

sections.title: Splitting Apart and Joining Back
sections.body:
`split()` cuts a string into a **list** of pieces. With no argument it splits on runs of whitespace and discards the empty pieces, which makes it the tidy way to get the words out of a messy line. Give it a separator, as in `"a,b".split(",")`, and it cuts on exactly that instead - keeping empty pieces where two separators touch.

A list is indexed with the same square brackets a string is, so `parts[0]` is the first piece and `parts[-1]` the last, and `len(parts)` counts them.

Going the other way, `sep.join(pieces)` glues the pieces into one string with `sep` between each pair. Note which side is which: the separator is the string you call `.join` on, and the pieces are the argument.
sections.code:
line = "  fire   ice  wind "
parts = line.split()
print(parts)
print(len(parts))
print(parts[0])
print("-".join(parts))
print("a,b,,c".split(","))

annotations.text: No argument: split on any run of spaces and drop the empty pieces.
'-' is the glue, parts is what gets glued. Separators only go between.
With an explicit separator, the empty piece between the two commas is kept.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `count_words(text)` returning how many whitespace-separated words `text` contains.
checkpoint.explain: Splitting with no argument collapses runs of whitespace and drops the empty pieces, so the messy and the empty cases both fall out for free - no counting of spaces required.

sections.title: def, return, and the print Trap
sections.body:
A **function** packages work under a name. `def` names it, the parentheses list its **parameters**, and the indented block below is its body; calling it runs that body with your arguments bound to those parameter names.

`return` hands a value back to whoever called the function and ends the call there and then. `print` does something quite different: it writes text to the screen and hands nothing back.

A function that never reaches a `return` hands back `None`. That is the single most common beginner bug - the output looks right on screen, but the value you captured is `None` and blows up the moment you use it.
sections.code:
def shout(text):
    return text.upper() + "!"

def show(text):
    print(text.upper() + "!")

loud = shout("hello")
print(loud + " " + loud)
got = show("hello")
print(got)

annotations.text: return produces a value for the caller - nothing is displayed yet.
print displays a value and returns nothing at all.
Because shout returned a string, it can be used in an expression.
show only printed; its call evaluated to None, and that is what got holds.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `initial(name)` returning the first character of `name` in uppercase. Assume `name` is not empty.
checkpoint.explain: Indexing gives a one-character string, and upper() works on it like any other string. Printing it here would satisfy your eyes and fail every test, because the caller receives None.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: Index 0 is the first character, not the second - counting starts at zero. The -1 index saves you from writing spell[len(spell) - 1] every time you want the end.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the blanks so this prints `fire-bolt`.
guided-practice.explain: replace takes the old text first and the new text second, and it operates on whatever the previous call in the chain returned - so lowercasing before replacing means the replace only has to deal with one case of letters.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `add_prefix_un(word)` that returns `word` with `un` stuck on the front. `add_prefix_un('happy')` returns `'unhappy'`.
guided-practice.starterCode:
def add_prefix_un(word):
    pass
guided-practice.solution:
def add_prefix_un(word):
    return 'un' + word
guided-practice.hint: `+` joins two strings; the prefix goes on the left.
guided-practice.explain: Concatenation builds a brand new string rather than pushing characters into the old one - which is exactly why the empty-string case needs no special branch and simply produces the prefix alone.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: The second line does real work and then discards it: the new uppercase string is never stored anywhere. Nothing a string method does can ever reach back and alter the string it was called on.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `first_and_last(word)` returning a two-character string made of the first and last characters of `word`. Assume `word` is not empty, so `first_and_last('a')` returns `'aa'`.
guided-practice.starterCode:
def first_and_last(word):
    pass
guided-practice.solution:
def first_and_last(word):
    return word[0] + word[-1]
guided-practice.hint: Two indexes joined with +. What is the index of the last character?
guided-practice.explain: For a one-character word the two indexes 0 and -1 land on the same character, which is why 'a' doubles rather than failing. Reaching for len(word) - 1 works too but is longer and easier to get wrong by one.

guided-practice.prompt: `double_word` is supposed to hand back the word written twice so the caller can use it, but every test reports `None`. Fix it.
guided-practice.starterCode:
def double_word(word):
    print(word + word)
guided-practice.solution:
def double_word(word):
    return word + word
guided-practice.hint: The function shows the answer but never gives it back.
guided-practice.explain: Printing satisfies a human reader; returning satisfies the program. A function that falls off the end without a return evaluates to None, and None is what the test harness compared against your expected string.

guided-practice.prompt: Order these lines into a program that defines `tidy` and then prints `OK`.
guided-practice.explain: The header comes first, the body is indented under it, and the return has to come after the variable it uses exists. The call sits at the left margin because it is not part of the function - and it must follow the def, since Python runs top to bottom.

guided-practice.prompt: A line reading just `name.strip()` sits in the middle of a program, and afterwards `name` still has its spaces. State the rule that explains this.
guided-practice.explain: The stripped string really was built - it just had nowhere to live, so it was discarded on the spot. Once you internalise that every string method is a factory rather than an editor, a whole family of silent bugs disappears.

challenge-set.prompt: Write `replace_word_choice(sentence, old_word, new_word)` returning `sentence` with every occurrence of `old_word` swapped for `new_word`. If `old_word` never appears, return the sentence unchanged.
challenge-set.starterCode:
def replace_word_choice(sentence, old_word, new_word):
    pass
challenge-set.solution:
def replace_word_choice(sentence, old_word, new_word):
    return sentence.replace(old_word, new_word)
challenge-set.hint: One method does the whole job, and it replaces every occurrence by default.
challenge-set.explain: replace handles all occurrences, not just the first, and quietly returns an identical copy when there is no match - so the 'not found' case needs no guard. It matches raw substrings, not whole words, which is worth remembering before you replace 'cat' inside 'category'.

challenge-set.prompt: Write `remove_suffix_ness(word)` that strips the four-letter suffix `ness`. English spelling turned a final `y` into `i`, so restore it: `'heaviness'` becomes `'heavy'` while `'sadness'` becomes `'sad'`.
challenge-set.hint: word[:-4] drops the last four characters. Then look at what the new last character is.
challenge-set.explain: A negative end index counts from the right, so word[:-4] means 'everything except the last four'. Testing root[-1:] rather than root[-1] is what keeps the bare 'ness' case from raising an IndexError - a one-character slice of an empty string is just an empty string.

challenge-set.prompt: `domain(email)` must return the part after the `@`, and an empty string when there is no `@` at all. It currently keeps the `@`, and returns the whole address when the `@` is missing. Fix both faults.
challenge-set.hint: find returns -1 when the substring is absent, and -1 is a perfectly valid index.
challenge-set.explain: The two faults share one root: a slice that starts at the found index includes the separator, and the sentinel -1 is not an error value to Python - it is the last character, so the slice silently returns everything. Checking for -1 before slicing is the habit that makes find safe.

challenge-set.prompt: Give the value bound to each name after its line runs. Write strings without quotes; write the list exactly as Python would display it.
challenge-set.code:
raw = "  Fire Bolt  "
a = raw.strip()
b = a.lower()
c = b.split()
d = "-".join(c)
challenge-set.explain: Every line consumes the previous value and produces a fresh one, and the type changes halfway through: split turns one string into a list of them, join turns a list back into one string. Naming each intermediate is how you catch a chain that silently lost a piece.

challenge-set.prompt: This code crashes on the last line with `TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "NoneType") to str`. Explain what `tidy` actually gives back and what one change fixes it.
challenge-set.explain: The stripped text was displayed and then dropped; the call itself evaluated to None, and None cannot be concatenated with a string. The reason the error is confusing is that the correct text appeared on screen a moment earlier - proof that printing and returning are different acts.

challenge-set.prompt: Vocabulary drill: `make_word_groups(text)` takes a string whose first word is a prefix, and returns the prefix followed by each remaining word with the prefix applied, separated by ` :: `. `make_word_groups('en close joy lighten')` returns `'en :: enclose :: enjoy :: enlighten'`. Do it without a loop.
challenge-set.hint: The separator can be more than punctuation. What if the glue itself carried the prefix?
challenge-set.explain: The trick is realising the separator is just a string you get to build: making the glue ' :: ' + prefix applies the prefix to every word after the first, because join only inserts between pieces. That is also why a single word comes back untouched - there is no gap to fill.

exam.prompt: What does `"fireball".find("ice")` evaluate to?
exam.explain: find reports absence with the sentinel -1 rather than raising, which is convenient until you forget to check it: -1 is also a legal index, so the mistake shows up as wrong data instead of a crash.

exam.prompt: Which of these expressions evaluate to `True`?
exam.explain: `in` finds a substring anywhere, not just at the start, so both halves match. It is case-sensitive, which is why the capitalised one fails - lowercase both sides first when you want a case-blind search.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.code:
s = "grimoire"
print(s[:3])
print(s[-4:])
print(s[3:3] == "")
print(len(s[2:5]))
exam.explain: An empty start or end means 'from the beginning' or 'to the end'. A slice whose bounds are equal spans nothing at all, and the length of any slice s[a:b] within range is simply b - a.

exam.prompt: Fill the blanks so this prints `a-b-c`.
exam.explain: The separator is the string you call join on, and the pieces are its argument - the reverse of what most people guess. split runs first because join needs the list of pieces before it can glue anything.

exam.prompt: In two or three sentences, state the difference between `return` and `print` inside a function, and say what a function without a `return` gives back.
exam.explain: One communicates with the program, the other with the person watching. Getting this backwards produces code that looks correct while every value it hands on is None - and None only fails later, far from the function that caused it.

exam.prompt: Write `check_sentence_ending(sentence)` returning `True` when `sentence` ends with a full stop `.` and `False` otherwise. An empty sentence is `False`.
exam.starterCode:
def check_sentence_ending(sentence):
    pass

tests.input: 'I like to hike, bake, and read.'

exam.solution:
def check_sentence_ending(sentence):
    return sentence[-1:] == "."
exam.hint: A one-character slice of the end is safe even when there is no end to speak of.
exam.explain: Comparing sentence[-1:] instead of sentence[-1] is what makes the empty case return False rather than raising an IndexError, because slicing out of range is permitted while indexing out of range is not. Returning the comparison directly is better than an if that returns True or False - the comparison is already the bool you want.

exam.prompt: `initials` should turn a full name into uppercase initials with a dot after each, so `'mira vex'` gives `'M.V.'`. It keeps the original letter case. Fix it.
exam.hint: Every other part of the function is already correct - only the letters are wrong.
exam.explain: parts[0][0] is a double index: the first word, then the first character of that word - and a one-character string still has all the string methods. The messy spacing case already passes untouched because split() with no argument collapses runs of whitespace for you.

exam.prompt: Order these lines into a program that defines `last_word` and prints the last word of a sentence.
exam.explain: A name has to exist before it is used, so the split must run before the return - and nothing after a return in the same block would ever execute anyway. The call is unindented because it belongs to the program, not the function.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.code:
def tag(word):
    print("<" + word + ">")

result = tag("fire")
print(result)
exam.explain: Two lines appear even though only one print is inside the function: the second comes from printing what the call produced. Reaching the end of a body without a return is not an error, it just yields None.

exam.prompt: Write `slugify(title)` that turns a title into a URL slug: trim the outer whitespace, drop one trailing full stop `.` if there is one, lowercase everything, and join the words with single `-` characters. `slugify('  Fire   Bolt. ')` returns `'fire-bolt'`, and an empty title returns an empty string.
exam.starterCode:
def slugify(title):
    pass
exam.hint: Deal with the full stop while the string is still one piece, then let split and join handle the spacing.
exam.explain: Order is the whole design here: the full stop has to go before you split, or it clings to the last word, and split-then-join beats replacing spaces because it collapses runs of whitespace instead of producing a row of hyphens. The safe slice text[-1:] once again lets the empty title travel the same path as every other input, with no special case.

sections.title: A Row of Boxes
sections.body:
A **list** is an ordered row of values written in square brackets, and it can hold anything - numbers, strings, even other lists.

Each slot has an **index** counting from `0`, while negative indices count backwards from the end, so `xs[-1]` is always the last item.

A **slice** `xs[start:stop]` copies out a new list running from `start` up to but not including `stop`, and `len(xs)` reports how many items the list holds.

The `in` operator asks whether a value sits somewhere in the list and answers `True` or `False`.
sections.code:
loot = ["sword", "torch", "rope", "gem"]
print(loot[0], loot[-1])
print(loot[1:3])
print(len(loot))
print("rope" in loot)

annotations.text: Index 0 is the first slot and -1 is the last, so you never need len(loot) - 1 to reach the end.
The slice stops before index 3, so you get items 1 and 2 only - two items, not three.
`in` searches by value and gives back a bool, not a position.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.explain: In a four-item list, counting 2 forward and 2 backward lands on the same slot - that is why `xs[-1]` and `xs[len(xs) - 1]` are interchangeable. A single index hands back the bare value, but a slice always hands back a list, even a one-item one.

sections.title: Reshaping the Row
sections.body:
Lists are **mutable**, so the methods below change the list you already have instead of handing you a new one.

`append(x)` adds to the end, `insert(i, x)` pushes an item in at index `i`, `pop()` removes **and returns** the last item (or the item at an index you pass it), and `remove(x)` deletes the first occurrence of a value.

`sort()` and `reverse()` also rearrange in place and evaluate to `None`, which is why `xs = xs.sort()` destroys your data - `sorted(xs)` is the version that leaves the original alone and returns a new list.

Because `remove(x)` raises `ValueError` when the value is absent, check `x in xs` first.
sections.code:
stack = [3, 1, 2]
stack.append(4)
stack.insert(0, 9)
print(stack)

taken = stack.pop()
stack.remove(1)
print(taken, stack)

print(sorted(stack))
stack.sort()
stack.reverse()
print(stack)

annotations.text: insert(0, 9) pushes 9 onto the front and shifts everything else right one slot.
pop is the one mutating method that hands the removed item back to you.
sorted() builds a new list; stack itself is still [9, 3, 2] on the next line.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.explain: Methods that mutate in place return `None` by convention, precisely so you cannot mistake a return value for the result. The work still happened - it happened to the list itself, which is what the second line reveals.

sections.title: For Each, and range
sections.body:
A `for` loop walks an **iterable** and binds each element in turn to your loop variable - it hands you the items, not their positions.

When you genuinely need numbers, `range(stop)` counts from `0`, and `range(start, stop, step)` lets you choose where to begin, where to stop and how far to jump; the `stop` value is never produced.

An **accumulator** is a variable created before the loop and updated inside it, which is how you build up a total or grow a list one element at a time.

Writing `total += n` is shorthand for `total = total + n`.
sections.code:
spells = ["ward", "bolt", "mend"]
for spell in spells:
    print(spell)

total = 0
for n in range(2, 11, 3):
    total += n
    print(n, total)

names = []
for i in range(len(spells)):
    names.append(str(i) + ":" + spells[i])
print(names)

annotations.text: spell is bound to each string in turn - there is no counter to manage.
range(2, 11, 3) yields 2, 5 and 8; 11 is the stop, so it never appears.
range(len(xs)) is how you loop over positions when you need the index itself.

checkpoint.prompt: Fill the blanks so this prints 10 - the sum of 1 through 4.
checkpoint.template:
total = 0
for n in ___(1, 5):
    total ___ n
print(total)
checkpoint.explain: The accumulator has to be initialised outside the loop or it would reset on every pass, and the upper bound is 5 because range stops one short of it.

sections.title: While, Break, Continue, Nest
sections.body:
A `while` loop repeats as long as its test is true, so **something in the body must move that test toward false** or the loop never ends.

An empty list is falsy and a non-empty one is truthy, which makes `while queue:` the idiomatic way to drain a list.

Inside any loop, `break` abandons the loop immediately and `continue` skips straight to the next iteration.

Loops also nest: for every single step of the outer loop, the inner loop runs all the way through.

annotations.text: The list itself is the test; each pop(0) shortens it until it is empty and falsy.
continue jumps straight to the next n without running the rest of the body.
break leaves the loop entirely, so 7 is never printed.
The inner loop restarts from scratch for each value of row: 2 x 3 = 6 lines.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.explain: The test is only checked between iterations, never mid-body, so the loop stops at the first value that fails it rather than at exactly 10. Overshooting a bound is normal for a stepped counter, and it is why `while n != 10` here would run forever.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: len counts items while an index selects one, and the two use different numbers for the same list: three items, but the last index is 2. Mixing them up is the source of nearly every IndexError.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the blanks so this adds "torch" to the end of the bag and then takes the last item back off. It prints: ['rope'] torch
guided-practice.template:
bag = ["rope"]
bag.___("torch")
last = bag.___()
print(bag, last)
guided-practice.explain: append and pop are a matched pair at the end of a list: one grows it and returns nothing, the other shrinks it and returns the item. That asymmetry is exactly why `last = bag.append(...)` would be wrong.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `total(xs)` returning the sum of every number in the list `xs`, using a loop. An empty list totals 0.
guided-practice.starterCode:
def total(xs):
    running = 0
    # loop over xs and add each value to running
    return running
guided-practice.hint: Create the accumulator before the loop, not inside it.
guided-practice.explain: Starting the accumulator at 0 outside the loop is what makes the empty list return 0 with no special case - the body simply never runs. Initialising it inside the loop would throw away everything added so far on every pass.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `middle(xs)` returning a new list containing everything except the first and last items. `middle([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])` is `[2, 3, 4]`. Lists of two items or fewer give back an empty list.
guided-practice.solution:
def middle(xs):
    return xs[1:-1]
guided-practice.hint: A slice can start at 1 and stop at -1.
guided-practice.explain: Slicing never raises for out-of-range bounds - it clamps to what actually exists, so the short lists fall out for free instead of needing a length check. That forgiveness is the practical difference between slicing and indexing.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.code:
scores = [3, 1, 2]
scores.append(4)
scores.reverse()
print(scores)
print(scores.pop(0))
print(scores)
guided-practice.explain: reverse works on whatever the list holds at that moment, so the freshly appended 4 is carried to the front rather than staying at the end. pop then both yields a value and shortens the list, which is why the third line differs from the first.

guided-practice.prompt: `evens_up_to(n)` should return every even number from 0 up to **and including** n. It currently drops the last one. Fix it.
guided-practice.hint: range never produces its stop value.
guided-practice.explain: range is half-open, so an inclusive upper bound has to be written as `stop + 1`. The fix stays safe for odd n: with 8 as the stop the sequence still ends at 6, because the step decides which values are ever reached.

challenge-set.prompt: This loop serves a queue one person at a time. Trace both lists.
challenge-set.explain: pop(0) takes from the front, so order is preserved as items move between the two lists. Nothing counts the iterations: the loop ends the moment queue becomes empty, because an empty list is falsy.

challenge-set.prompt: Write `above_threshold(scores, threshold)` returning a list of every score greater than **or equal to** the threshold, in the order they appear.
challenge-set.starterCode:
def above_threshold(scores, threshold):
    keep = []
    # test each score, keep the ones that qualify
    return keep
challenge-set.hint: Filtering is an accumulator that collects instead of adding.
challenge-set.explain: Appending inside the loop preserves the original order for free, which a sort or a set would destroy. The boundary is the real test here: `>=` keeps an exact match, so a score of 100 against a threshold of 100 must survive.

challenge-set.prompt: Arrange these fragments into a function that returns the largest value in a non-empty list.
challenge-set.explain: The accumulator is seeded with a real element rather than 0, otherwise a list of negative numbers would wrongly report 0 as its largest value. The return sits outside the loop, since returning inside it would stop after the very first comparison.

challenge-set.prompt: Write `remove_all(xs, item)` deleting **every** occurrence of `item` from `xs` and returning the list. Removing something that is not there must not raise.
challenge-set.hint: `while item in xs` is both the guard against ValueError and the loop condition.
challenge-set.explain: One membership test does double duty: it ends the loop and it guarantees remove never raises. A `for` loop over xs would be wrong for a subtler reason - deleting while iterating the same list shifts the remaining positions and silently skips elements.

challenge-set.prompt: `flatten(rows)` should return one flat list holding every item from every row, in order. Instead it hands back the rows unchanged. Fix it.
challenge-set.hint: Each row is itself a list, so it needs a loop of its own.
challenge-set.explain: append adds exactly one item, and a whole list counts as one item - nesting a second loop is what turns rows of values into values. An empty inner row costs nothing, because its loop body simply never runs.

challenge-set.prompt: Write `podium(scores)` returning the three highest scores in descending order. Fewer than three scores means you return however many there are.
challenge-set.solution:
def podium(scores):
    scores.sort()
    scores.reverse()
    return scores[:3]
challenge-set.hint: sort() then reverse() gives descending order, and a slice handles the short lists.
challenge-set.explain: Slicing past the end of a list is not an error, so `[:3]` covers the one- and two-score cases without any length check. Keep in mind that sort and reverse rewrite the caller's list - when that matters, start from `sorted(scores)` instead.

exam.prompt: What does `[10, 20, 30][-1]` evaluate to?
exam.explain: Negative indices count backwards from the end, with -1 meaning the last slot. That is the reason you almost never see `xs[len(xs) - 1]` in Python.

exam.prompt: Given `xs = [5, 3, 8]`, which call deletes the **value** 3?
exam.explain: remove takes a value while pop takes an index, so `pop(3)` reaches for a fourth slot that does not exist and `pop(-3)` drops the 5. Lists have no delete method at all.

exam.prompt: Which of these leave the original list `xs` unchanged?
exam.explain: The built-in function and the slice each build a new list, while the two methods rearrange in place. The shape of the call is the tell: a method called on the list usually edits that list.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: A negative step counts downwards and still refuses to produce the stop value, giving 10, 7, 4 and 1. break fires on 4 before the append runs, so that value never reaches the list.

exam.prompt: Fill the blanks so this prints each name once, taken from the front of the queue, until the queue is empty.
exam.explain: The list is its own condition: non-empty is truthy, empty is falsy. pop(0) is what eventually makes that condition fail, so a version that only read the front item would loop forever.

exam.prompt: Trace the value of `total` after each element has been visited.
exam.explain: continue skips the rest of the body but not the iteration itself, so the negative elements are still visited - they just leave the accumulator untouched. Naming the value at every step is how you catch a guard written on the wrong side of the update.

exam.prompt: A colleague writes `scores = scores.sort()` and every line after it crashes with `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute ...`. Explain what went wrong and how you would fix it.
exam.explain: sort did its job and then returned None, and the assignment threw the sorted list away by rebinding the name to that None. Either drop the assignment entirely, or call `sorted(scores)`, which is the version built for the value-returning case.

exam.prompt: Write `running_totals(xs)` returning a list of the running sum after each element. `running_totals([1, 2, 3])` is `[1, 3, 6]`.
exam.starterCode:
def running_totals(xs):
    out = []
    total = 0
    # after each element, record the total so far
    return out
exam.solution:
def running_totals(xs):
    out = []
    total = 0
    for x in xs:
        total += x
        out.append(total)
    return out
exam.hint: Two accumulators: one number, one list.
exam.explain: The number accumulator carries state across iterations while the list accumulator records a snapshot of it, which is why the output always has exactly as many items as the input. Appending before the update would shift every entry by one element.

exam.prompt: `every_other(xs)` should return the items at index 0, 2, 4 and so on. It returns the wrong half. Fix it.
exam.hint: The step is already right; the start is not.
exam.explain: The step controls the spacing and the start decides which half you land on, so only the start needed changing. Using `len(xs)` as the stop keeps every index legal for any length, including the empty list, where the loop simply never runs.

exam.prompt: Write `leaderboard(names, scores)` where both lists are already in ranking order and line up by position. Return a list of strings shaped `"1. Ana: 90"` - the rank counting from 1, then the name, a colon, a space and the score.
exam.starterCode:
def leaderboard(names, scores):
    rows = []
    # you need the position, not just the name
    return rows
exam.hint: range(len(names)) gives you i, and that one i indexes both lists.
exam.explain: When two lists are read in parallel you loop over positions rather than items, because a single index has to reach into both. The rank is `i + 1` for exactly the reason indices start at 0 - the display counts from one, the machine counts from zero.

exam.prompt: Write `merge_sorted(a, b)` taking two lists already sorted ascending and returning one sorted list holding every item from both. Do it by repeatedly taking the smaller front item - do not call sort().
exam.starterCode:
def merge_sorted(a, b):
    out = []
    # while both lists still have items, take the smaller front one
    # then drain whatever is left
    return out
exam.hint: Three while loops: one for the comparison phase, then one to drain each leftover list.
exam.explain: Only the two front items ever need comparing, because everything behind them is already larger - that single observation is what makes merging a walk rather than a re-sort. The drain loops matter because one list always empties first, and `<=` rather than `<` is what keeps equal values in their original relative order.

sections.title: Keys Instead of Positions
sections.body:
A **dict** maps keys to values, so you look a thing up by name instead of by position. Write one as comma-separated `key: value` pairs inside braces, and read a value back with `d[key]`.

Assigning to a key that does not exist creates it; assigning to one that already exists replaces its value. There is no separate add and update, and no `append`.

Asking for a key that is not there with `d[key]` raises a **KeyError**, which is why `in` matters - it asks whether a **key** is present, never a value.
sections.code:
spells = {"ember": 3, "frost": 5}
spells["gale"] = 2
print(spells["frost"])
print("ember" in spells)
print(len(spells))
print(spells)

annotations.text: A dict literal: comma-separated key: value pairs inside braces.
The key `gale` did not exist, so this assignment creates it.
`in` asks about keys only - `3 in spells` would be False even though 3 is a value.
Printing the whole dict shows insertion order: ember, frost, then the new gale.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.code:
runes = {"a": 1, "b": 2}
runes["c"] = 3
runes["a"] = 9
print(runes)
print("d" in runes)
checkpoint.explain: Reassigning an existing key edits it in place and keeps its original position, so `a` stays first even though it was written last. Only a brand-new key is appended at the end.

sections.title: Asking a Dictionary Politely
sections.body:
`d.get(key)` is the polite form of `d[key]` - it hands back `None` for a missing key instead of raising. Pass a second argument and that becomes the fallback, which is what turns counting into one line: `counts.get(word, 0) + 1`.

Three views let you walk a dict: `.keys()`, `.values()` and `.items()`.

`.items()` yields `(key, value)` pairs, so `for name, count in d.items()` splits each pair into two names as it goes.
sections.code:
loot = {"gold": 12, "silver": 3}
print(loot.get("gold"))
print(loot.get("copper"))
print(loot.get("copper", 0))
for name, count in loot.items():
    print(name, count)
print(sorted(loot.keys()))
print(sum(loot.values()))

annotations.text: A missing key gives None rather than raising KeyError.
The second argument is the value to use when the key is absent.
Each item is a pair, and the two names on the left take its two parts.
`.values()` is a plain collection of the values - sum, max and len all work on it.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `shelf_count(stock, item)` returning how many of `item` the dict `stock` holds, and `0` when the item is not in the dict at all.
checkpoint.explain: The default argument removes the `if item in stock` branch entirely, so the absent case and the present case travel the same path. That is why `.get` shows up in almost every counting loop.

sections.title: Sets Forget Duplicates
sections.body:
A **set** is an unordered collection that stores each value once, written with braces around bare values. Building one from any sequence deduplicates it in a single pass, and `in` on a set is a direct membership test rather than a scan.

Sets carry the three operations from school maths - `|` union, `&` intersection, `-` difference - and each returns a new set.

Two traps: `{}` is an empty **dict**, so the empty set must be written `set()`; and a set has no order, so wrap it in `sorted(...)` whenever you need a predictable result.

annotations.text: The duplicate collapses on the way in - the set holds two values, not three.
Adding something already present is a no-op, not an error.
Union, intersection, difference. sorted() is only here to make the output deterministic.
`{}` is an empty dict; the empty set has no literal and must be written set().

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.code:
tags = ["red", "blue", "red", "green"]
unique = set(tags)
print(len(unique))
print(sorted(unique))
print("blue" in unique)
checkpoint.explain: Four items go in and three come out because the second `red` has nowhere to live. Sorting is what makes the middle line predictable - the raw set has no order to print.

sections.title: Tuples, Unpacking and the Swap
sections.body:
A **tuple** is a fixed sequence written with commas, usually inside parentheses. It is **immutable**: you can read `point[0]`, but assigning to it raises a `TypeError`.

That restriction is the feature. A value that cannot change can be a dict key or a set member, which is exactly why a list cannot be either.

**Unpacking** spreads a tuple across several names at once, and the count of names must match the count of items. Because Python builds the whole right-hand side before binding anything on the left, `a, b = b, a` swaps two names with no temporary variable.
sections.code:
point = (3, 7)
x, y = point
print(x + y)
a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)
pairs = [("ash", 2), ("ember", 5)]
for name, count in pairs:
    print(name, count)
print({(0, 0): "origin"}[(0, 0)])
try:
    point[0] = 99
except TypeError as err:
    print("TypeError:", err)

annotations.text: Unpacking: the names on the left line up with the items on the right.
The right side (b, a) is built first, so nothing is overwritten mid-swap.
A tuple can be a dict key because it can never change; a list cannot.
Immutable means exactly this - item assignment is not available, ever.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `swap(pair)` that takes a two-item tuple and returns a new tuple holding the same two items in the opposite order. Unpack the pair rather than indexing it.
checkpoint.explain: You cannot rearrange the tuple you were handed, so the only move is to build a new one. Unpacking names the parts, and `return b, a` packs them straight back into a tuple without any parentheses.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print?
guided-practice.explain: Indexing a dict asks for a value by its key, while `len` counts key-value pairs, not values. Reading 5 then 2 is the difference between looking inside and looking at the whole.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the blanks so `stock` returns the recorded count for `name`, or 0 when the dict has no such key.
guided-practice.explain: Without the second argument this returns `None` for a missing key, and `None` cannot be added to anything. Supplying the fallback is what makes the result safe to do arithmetic on.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print?
guided-practice.explain: The gap between the first two numbers is the count of duplicates the set discarded. Sorting afterwards is required because a set has no order of its own to print.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `letter_set(word)` returning a sorted list of the distinct characters in `word`. `letter_set('banana')` returns `['a', 'b', 'n']`.
guided-practice.starterCode:
def letter_set(word):
    pass
guided-practice.solution:
def letter_set(word):
    return sorted(set(word))
guided-practice.hint: A string is a sequence of characters, so set() accepts one directly.
guided-practice.explain: Iterating a string yields characters, so `set(word)` deduplicates without a loop. The last test is a reminder that sorting is by code point, which puts every capital letter before every lowercase one.

guided-practice.prompt: Order these fragments into a function that counts how many times each item appears.
guided-practice.explain: The accumulator has to be created before the loop, or every pass would start from an empty dict again. The `return` sits outside the loop because the answer is only complete once every item has been seen.

guided-practice.prompt: Two points are given as `(x, y)` tuples. Write `distance_apart(a, b)` returning the number of grid steps between them: the size of the x difference plus the size of the y difference.
guided-practice.hint: x1, y1 = a gives the first point two readable names.
guided-practice.explain: Unpacking each point into named coordinates makes the formula read like the sentence it came from, where `a[0] - b[0]` reads like an index puzzle. `abs` is what stops the two differences cancelling each other out.

challenge-set.prompt: `tally(items)` should count how many times each item appears, but it raises `KeyError` on the very first item. Fix it so the tests pass.
challenge-set.hint: The right-hand side reads a key that has not been created yet.
challenge-set.explain: The first sighting of an item is also the moment its key does not exist yet, so the read fails before the write can help. Supplying `0` as the default makes the first sighting behave like every later one.

challenge-set.prompt: The loop below runs over `items = ['ash', 'ember', 'ash']`. Give the full contents of `counts` after each pass, written exactly as Python would print the dict.
challenge-set.explain: Watching the dict grow shows the two distinct events a counting loop mixes together: creating a key with the default, and bumping one that is already there. The repeat updates in place, so the printed order never changes after a key first appears.

challenge-set.prompt: Write `set_report(a, b)` taking two lists and returning a tuple of three sorted lists: the values in both, the values only in `a`, and the values only in `b`. `set_report([1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 4])` returns `([2, 3], [1], [4])`.
challenge-set.hint: & is intersection and - is difference; note that a - b and b - a are different sets.
challenge-set.explain: Difference is not symmetric, which is why the answer needs both `a - b` and `b - a` rather than one of them. Returning three values at once packs them into a tuple, so the caller can unpack them into three names in a single line.

challenge-set.prompt: `{(0, 0): 'origin'}` is a valid dict, but `{[0, 0]: 'origin'}` raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'`. Explain what property of a tuple lets it be a key, and what would go wrong if lists were allowed as keys.
challenge-set.explain: A dict finds a key by its hash, and that hash is computed from the value's contents. If the contents could change after storage the entry would be filed in a place nobody could ever look, so Python refuses mutable values as keys instead of letting them go missing.

challenge-set.prompt: You are given a list of `(name, score)` tuples. Write `rank_by_score(pairs)` returning a new list of the same tuples ordered by score, lowest first, with equal scores broken alphabetically by name. `rank_by_score([('ash', 3), ('ember', 1)])` returns `[('ember', 1), ('ash', 3)]`.
challenge-set.hint: Build (score, name) tuples, sort those, then unpack them back the other way round.
challenge-set.explain: Tuples compare item by item, so sorting `(score, name)` gives you the primary and tie-break rules for free without writing a comparison at all. Unpacking on the way in and repacking on the way out is the whole trick - the ordering logic is the tuple's, not yours.

challenge-set.prompt: Write `group_by_first_letter(words)` returning a dict whose keys are first letters and whose values are the sorted lists of words starting with that letter. `group_by_first_letter(['ash', 'ember', 'ale'])` returns `{'a': ['ale', 'ash'], 'e': ['ember']}`. Assume no word is empty.
challenge-set.hint: Check membership with `if letter not in groups` before appending.
challenge-set.explain: A dict of lists needs the empty list created before the first append, which is the same missing-key problem as counting, solved with `in` instead of `.get` because the default here has to be a fresh list each time. Sorting at the end keeps the answer independent of the order the words arrived in.

level-project.prompt:
Build the floor's word frequency counter.

Write `word_frequency(text)` returning a dict that maps each word to the number of times it appears. Split the text on whitespace with `text.split()`. From each piece, strip the characters `.,!?;:` off both ends with `raw.strip(PUNCTUATION)`, then lowercase it, so `Hello,` and `hello` are the same word. Skip any piece that is empty once stripped. Text with no words at all returns an empty dict.
level-project.hint: counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1 handles the first sighting and every repeat with one line.
level-project.explain: Normalising each token before it reaches the dict is what collapses `Hello,` and `HELLO` onto one key - counting first and cleaning afterwards cannot be repaired. The empty cases fall out for free rather than needing a guard, because a loop over nothing simply never runs and returns the dict it started with.

exam.prompt: `prices = {'ink': 3}`. What is the value of `prices.get('quill')`?
exam.explain: `.get` never raises - it substitutes a value, and with no second argument that value is `None`. That is exactly why `.get(key, 0)` exists: `None + 1` would fail just as loudly as the KeyError you were avoiding.

exam.prompt: What does `len({1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3})` evaluate to?
exam.explain: Deduplication happens as the literal is built, not when it is read, so the repeats never occupy space to be counted. Six values are written and three survive.

exam.prompt: What does this program print?
exam.explain: Each item arrives as a pair and is unpacked into two names by the loop header, which is why `print` receives two separate arguments rather than a tuple. `.values()` hands `sum` the numbers alone, with no keys in the way.

exam.prompt: What does this program print?
exam.explain: The two difference lines print different answers, which is the point: subtraction of sets has a direction. Union counts each value once, so the four distinct values across both sets give 4 rather than 6.

exam.prompt: Fill the blanks so this swaps the two values and prints `2 1`.
exam.template:
a = 1
b = 2
___, ___ = b, a
print(a, b)
exam.explain: The right side is evaluated into a tuple before any name on the left is touched, so neither old value is lost part-way through. Writing it as two separate assignments would clobber `a` before `b` could read it.

exam.prompt: Which of these expressions may be used as a dictionary key?
exam.explain: Tuples and strings are immutable, so their hash is stable for as long as they exist. Lists and sets can be changed after they are stored, which would strand the entry in a bucket nobody could find again.

exam.prompt: Order these fragments into a function that removes duplicates while keeping first-seen order.
exam.explain: The set answers `have I seen this` and the list remembers `in what order`, and neither structure can do both jobs alone. Recording into `seen` has to happen inside the `if`, or the guard would never fire.

exam.prompt: Give the values of `(a, b, c)` after each line of this program, written as a tuple such as `(1, 2, 3)`.
exam.code:
a, b, c = 1, 2, 3
a, b = b, a
b, c = c, b
exam.explain: Each line packs the right-hand side into a tuple first and only then unpacks it into the names, so the third line moves the old `c` into `b` and the old `b` into `c` simultaneously. Reading these as two sequential assignments instead is what produces the wrong final answer.

exam.prompt: `counts[key]` and `counts.get(key, 0)` behave differently when the key is absent. Describe the difference, and say which you would choose inside a counting loop and which you would choose when an unknown key means the program has a bug.
exam.explain: The choice is about whether an absent key is expected or is evidence of a mistake. Silencing the failure inside a counting loop is right because the first sighting is normal, but silencing it everywhere converts a loud bug into a quiet wrong answer.

exam.prompt: `bump(pair)` should return a pair whose second item is one larger, leaving the original alone. It raises `TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment`. Fix it.
exam.hint: You cannot edit a tuple, so build a new one from its parts.
exam.explain: No amount of rewriting makes item assignment work on a tuple - the fix is to stop trying to mutate and start returning a new value. Unpacking to two names and repacking them is the standard shape for editing anything immutable.

exam.prompt: Two ledgers are given as lists of `(name, amount)` tuples. Write `merge_ledgers(a, b)` returning a tuple of two things: a dict mapping each name to the sum of all its amounts across both ledgers, and a sorted list of the names that appear in both ledgers. `merge_ledgers([('ash', 2), ('ember', 3)], [('ash', 5)])` returns `({'ash': 7, 'ember': 3}, ['ash'])`.
