exam.hint: One dict for the sums, one set of names per ledger, and & for the overlap.
exam.explain: Every structure on this floor earns its place here: the dict accumulates by key, the sets answer the membership question the dict cannot, and unpacking the tuples is what lets the loop read like the data. Note that a total of 0 is not the same as an absent name, which is why the overlap must be computed from the names seen rather than from the totals.

lesson.title: Objects That Remember, Sequences That Wait

sections.title: A Class Is a Blueprint
sections.body:
A **class** describes a kind of thing; calling it, like `Potion("Elixir", 3)`, builds one **instance** of that kind. Python hands the fresh object to `__init__` as its first parameter, conventionally named **`self`**, and whatever you store on `self` becomes that instance's own data - its **instance attributes**.

A **method** is just a function defined inside the class, and it too receives the instance as `self`, which is how it reads and changes the object it was called on.

Two instances built from the same class share the blueprint but never the data: each has its own `self`.
sections.code:
class Potion:
    def __init__(self, name, charges):
        self.name = name
        self.charges = charges

    def sip(self):
        self.charges -= 1
        return self.charges


elixir = Potion("Elixir", 3)
tonic = Potion("Tonic", 1)
print(elixir.name, elixir.charges)
print(elixir.sip())
print(elixir.charges, tonic.charges)

annotations.text: Runs automatically on construction. It furnishes the object; it never returns one.
Stores the argument onto this instance, so it outlives the call.
`sip` changes the object it was called on, not a copy.
Two separate instances, each with its own charges.

checkpoint.prompt: Write a class `Torch` whose `__init__(self, fuel)` stores `self.fuel`, plus a method `burn()` that subtracts 1 from `self.fuel`. Then write `torch_after(fuel, times)` which builds a `Torch`, calls `burn()` that many times, and returns the fuel left.
checkpoint.explain: `__init__` does not create the object, it furnishes one that already exists - which is why it stores onto `self` instead of returning anything. Each `Torch(...)` call gets its own `self.fuel`, so burning one torch never touches another.
checkpoint.hint: Inside a method, the object you were called on is always the first parameter: self.

sections.title: Two Ways to Show an Object
sections.body:
By default, printing an object gives you something like `<__main__.Potion object at 0x7f2a>` - true, and useless. Two **dunder** (double-underscore) methods fix that: **`__str__`** is the readable form used by `print`, `str()` and f-strings, while **`__repr__`** is the precise form used by the interactive prompt and by any container holding the object.

Both must **return** a string rather than print one. If you write only `__repr__`, `str()` quietly falls back to it - but the fallback never runs the other way, which is why `__repr__` is the one to write if you write only one.

annotations.text: The human-facing form: print and f-strings reach for this.
`!r` formats with repr, so the name comes out quoted.
A list formats its elements with repr, never with str.

checkpoint.prompt: This class defines `__repr__` but no `__str__`. What does it print?
checkpoint.explain: `str()` falls back to `__repr__` when no `__str__` exists, but the fallback never runs the other way. That asymmetry is why `__repr__` is the one worth writing first.

sections.title: Equality and Length You Define
sections.body:
Without help, `==` between two objects asks *are these the same object?*, so two identically built instances come out unequal. Defining **`__eq__`** replaces that with your own rule - usually comparing the attributes that matter - and defining **`__len__`** makes `len(obj)` work.

One bonus follows for free: an object with `__len__` and no `__bool__` is falsy exactly when its length is zero, so an empty bundle behaves like an empty list in an `if`.

Guard `__eq__` with an `isinstance` check when the object might be compared against unrelated types.

annotations.text: Your rule for ==. Compare the state that defines the value.
`isinstance(other, Bundle)` first, so comparing against a string answers False instead of crashing.
Must return a non-negative integer; len() looks this up by name.
`is` still asks about identity, and no dunder can change that.
Truthiness falls back to __len__, so an empty Bundle is falsy.

checkpoint.prompt: Fill the blanks so two decks with the same cards compare equal and `len(deck)` counts the cards.
checkpoint.explain: `==` on the two attribute lists is what turns identity comparison into value comparison, and the dunder name is what `len()` looks up - the method is never called directly by name.

sections.title: Generators: Values On Demand
sections.body:
A function whose body contains **`yield`** is a **generator function**: calling it runs none of the body and hands back a generator object instead. Each `next()` resumes the body, runs to the next `yield`, hands that value out, and freezes the frame - local variables intact - until you ask again.

That is **laziness**: values are produced one at a time, on demand, so a generator over ten million rows costs one row of memory rather than ten million. It also makes an endless `while True` sequence safe, because nothing is produced until someone asks for it. Any function containing `yield` is a generator, including a method inside a class.
sections.code:
def countdown(n):
    print("body started")
    while n > 0:
        yield n
        n -= 1


gen = countdown(3)
print("generator made, nothing has run yet")
print(next(gen))
print(next(gen))
print(list(gen))

annotations.text: This line does not run until the first next() call.
Hands a value out and freezes here; the next resume starts on the line below.
Builds the generator. No part of the body has run yet.
Drains whatever is left - the first two values are already spent.

checkpoint.prompt: Write a generator function `first_letters(words)` that yields the first character of each word in `words`. It must use `yield`, not build a list.
checkpoint.explain: The tests wrap the call in `list()` because a generator is not a list - it is a promise to produce values when asked. Wrapping it is how you force every value out at once.
checkpoint.hint: Loop over words and yield word[0].

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.code:
class Lamp:
    def __init__(self, oil):
        self.oil = oil


a = Lamp(5)
b = Lamp(2)
print(a.oil)
print(b.oil)
a.oil = 9
print(a.oil, b.oil)
guided-practice.explain: Two calls to `Lamp(...)` build two separate objects, each with its own `oil` attribute stored on `self`. Rebinding one instance's attribute cannot reach the other - that separateness is the whole point of instances.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the blanks so `Counter(10)` builds an object whose `bump()` returns 11.
guided-practice.explain: Python calls `__init__` for you the moment the object is constructed, and the object being furnished arrives as the first parameter. Storing onto that parameter is what makes the value survive past the end of the method.

guided-practice.prompt: Write a class `Vault` with `__init__(self, gold)` storing `self.gold`, a method `deposit(amount)` that adds to it, and a method `balance()` returning the current gold. Then write `run_vault(start, deposits)` which builds a `Vault` with `start`, deposits every amount in the list, and returns `balance()`.
guided-practice.explain: The state lives on the object, so the loop can call `deposit` repeatedly without threading a running total through the caller. That is the trade a class makes: the caller stops carrying data around, and the object carries it instead.
guided-practice.hint: deposit changes self.gold; balance only reads it.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: `print`, `str()` and an f-string placeholder all reach for the same hook, so defining `__str__` once changes every one of them. There is no separate formatting rule for f-strings to learn.

guided-practice.prompt: Write a class `Card` with `__init__(self, rank, suit)` storing both, and a `__str__` that returns the card as `"<rank> of <suit>"` - for example `str(Card('A', 'spades'))` is `'A of spades'`.
guided-practice.explain: An f-string calls `str()` on whatever you interpolate, so the integer rank in the last test is converted for you - concatenating with `+` would have raised a TypeError instead. `__str__` must return a string, never print one.
guided-practice.hint: Return an f-string; do not print it.

guided-practice.prompt: This class does not define `__eq__`. What does it print?
guided-practice.code:
class Pair:
    def __init__(self, a, b):
        self.a = a
        self.b = b


p = Pair(1, 2)
q = Pair(1, 2)
print(p == q)
print(p == p)
print(p.a == q.a)
guided-practice.explain: Without `__eq__`, `==` on objects means *the same object*, not *the same contents* - so two identically built pairs are unequal while the ints inside them are equal. Value equality is something you opt into.

guided-practice.prompt: Write a class `Shelf` with `__init__(self, books)` storing a copy of the list, a `__len__` returning how many books it holds, and an `__eq__` that is true when the other shelf holds the same books in the same order. Then write `compare(a_books, b_books)` returning the tuple `(len(shelf_a), shelf_a == shelf_b)`.
guided-practice.explain: Comparing the two lists inside `__eq__` makes order matter for free, because list equality is already order-sensitive - the second test would pass if you compared sets instead. `__len__` must return a non-negative integer, which is exactly what delegating to `len(self.books)` guarantees.
guided-practice.hint: Both dunders can delegate to the list you stored.

guided-practice.prompt: Order these lines into a generator function that yields 0, 2, 4, ... up to but not including `limit`.
guided-practice.explain: The counter has to be initialised before the loop tests it, and the increment must sit after the `yield` - put it before and the value handed out is already one step stale. Execution resumes on the line after `yield`, which is why that ordering matters.

challenge-set.prompt: Calling `run(0, [1, 2, 3])` raises `NameError: name 'self' is not defined`. Fix the class without changing `run`.
challenge-set.explain: `self` is not a keyword - it is simply the name you give the first parameter, and Python passes the instance into it whether you declared it or not. Omitting it means `count` receives the instance and the name `self` never exists, which is exactly what the NameError reports.
challenge-set.hint: Count the parameters Python actually passes to __init__.

challenge-set.prompt: `describe(['ruby'])` should return `"[a ruby gem]"`, but it returns something like `"[<__main__.Gem object at 0x7f0>]"`. Fix the class so the list renders the gems.
challenge-set.explain: A container never calls `__str__` on the things inside it - it calls `__repr__`, so a class with only `__str__` looks fine when printed alone and turns into memory addresses the moment it is put in a list. Defining `__repr__` fixes both cases at once, because `str()` falls back to it.
challenge-set.hint: Which hook does a list use for its elements?

challenge-set.prompt: Conda Airlines seats four passengers per row, lettered `A`, `B`, `C`, `D`, then starts again at `A`. Write a generator function `generate_seat_letters(number)` that yields exactly `number` seat letters in that repeating order.
challenge-set.starterCode:
def generate_seat_letters(number):
    pass
challenge-set.explain: Indexing with `% 4` turns an ever-growing counter into a cycle, which is the standard way to repeat a fixed pattern without tracking where you are. Because it yields, a request for a million letters costs one letter of memory rather than a million-element list.
challenge-set.hint: range(number) plus the remainder operator gives you the cycle.

challenge-set.prompt: `gen = ticks(3)` has just run. Give the value of each following expression, in order. If the expression raises, name the exception.
challenge-set.explain: Each `next` resumes the frozen loop, runs to the next `yield`, and freezes again with `i` intact - the generator remembers its own place. When the loop finally ends, the generator raises `StopIteration`, which is the signal a `for` loop quietly catches for you.

challenge-set.prompt: A colleague changes `def rows(): return [parse(line) for line in log]` into a generator that yields each parsed line. Peak memory drops from gigabytes to almost nothing, but a second `for` loop over the same result now finds nothing at all. Explain both effects.
challenge-set.explain: Both effects come from the same fact: a generator holds a position, not a collection. Nothing is stored, so memory stays flat; and the position only moves forward, so once it reaches the end there is nothing left to replay - you must call the generator function again, or materialise it with `list()`, to iterate twice.

challenge-set.prompt: Write a class `Deck` with `__init__(self, cards)` storing a copy of the list, and a generator method `deal()` that yields each card in order. `list(Deck([1, 2, 3]).deal())` must give `[1, 2, 3]`.
challenge-set.explain: A method is a generator for exactly the same reason a function is - its body contains `yield` - and `self` stays alive inside the paused frame, so the method can keep reading the object's state between resumes. Dealing lazily means a table of a million cards never has to be copied to hand out the first one.
challenge-set.hint: The yield goes inside the method's loop.

challenge-set.prompt: Fill the blanks so this endless generator can be asked for its first value without hanging.
challenge-set.template:
def evens():
    n = 0
    while True:
        ___ n
        n += 2


gen = evens()
print(___(gen))
challenge-set.explain: `while True` only runs forever if something forces it to; a generator pauses at each hand-off, so an endless sequence is safe as long as you take a finite number of values from it. Swap in `list(gen)` and the same program never terminates.

challenge-set.prompt: Write a class `Playlist` with `__init__(self, tracks)` storing its own copy of the list, a method `add(track)`, a `__len__`, and an `__eq__` that is true when another playlist holds the same tracks in the same order. Then write `build(tracks, extra)` which makes a `Playlist` from `tracks`, adds every item of `extra` to it, and returns the tuple `(len(playlist), playlist == Playlist(tracks))`.
challenge-set.explain: `self.tracks = tracks` would alias the caller's list, so `add` would silently grow the very list the second `Playlist` is built from and the comparison would come out true every time. Copying with `list(tracks)` at construction is what keeps an object's state its own.
challenge-set.hint: Store list(tracks), not tracks.

exam.prompt: In `def sip(self):`, what is `self`?
choices: A Python keyword that always refers to the class
The first parameter, into which Python passes the instance the method was called on
A copy of the object, so changes to it are discarded when the method ends
The class itself, shared by every instance
exam.explain: Nothing about the name is special - `self` is a convention. What is real is the call protocol: `obj.sip()` becomes `Class.sip(obj)`, so the instance always arrives as the first argument and mutating it mutates the original.

exam.prompt: A class defines `__str__` but not `__repr__`. You put one instance in a list and print the list. What appears?
exam.explain: Containers format their elements with `repr`, and the fallback only runs the other direction: missing `__str__` borrows `__repr__`, never the reverse. This is the concrete reason `__repr__` is the one to define if you only define one.

exam.prompt: Which of these are true of a function whose body contains `yield`?
choices: Calling it runs the body immediately and returns the final value
Calling it returns a generator without executing the body
Each `next()` resumes execution just after the last `yield`
It can describe an endless sequence without hanging when partially consumed
Its local variables are discarded between `next()` calls
exam.explain: A generator is a paused stack frame, which is what makes the middle two statements true and the last one false - locals survive the pause. Because nothing runs until asked, an infinite loop inside is harmless until someone asks for every value.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, label):
        self.label = label
        self.links = []


a = Node("a")
b = Node("b")
a.links.append(b)
print(len(a.links), len(b.links))
print(a.links[0].label)
exam.explain: Because the empty list is created inside `__init__`, every node gets a fresh one - appending to `a.links` leaves `b.links` untouched. Had the list been created once at class level instead, both nodes would share it and the first line would read `1 1`.

exam.prompt: Fill the blanks so `len(Basket(['fig']))` is 1 and two baskets with the same fruit compare equal.
exam.explain: `__len__` delegating to the built-in `len` of the stored list is not circular - the outer call looks up the dunder, the inner call runs on a plain list. Reaching for `other.fruit` is what makes the comparison read the other object's state rather than its identity.

exam.prompt: What does this print? Pay attention to the interleaving.
exam.explain: `loud(2)` runs none of the body, which is why `before` prints first. After that the producing and consuming lines alternate, because each turn of the `for` loop drives the generator forward by exactly one `yield`.

exam.prompt: `list(evens_below(7))` should give `[0, 2, 4, 6]` but raises `TypeError: 'int' object is not iterable`. Fix it.
exam.explain: `return` ends the function for good and hands back one plain value, so the increment after it was unreachable and the caller got an int instead of something to iterate. `yield` hands a value out and keeps the frame alive, which is the only difference that matters here.
exam.hint: One keyword ends the function; the other pauses it.

exam.prompt: Write a class `Duration` with `__init__(self, minutes)` storing `self.minutes`, and a `__str__` returning the duration as hours and minutes in the form `"1h30m"`.
exam.explain: Floor division and remainder are the pair that splits one quantity into two units, and keeping that arithmetic inside `__str__` means the object still stores a single honest number. Storing hours and minutes as two attributes instead would let them drift out of step.
exam.hint: // gives whole hours, % gives what is left over.

exam.prompt: Give the value of `s.items` after each statement runs, written as a Python list.
exam.explain: Every method reaches the same list through `self`, so the object's state is a single thing changing over time rather than values being passed back and forth. Notice `pop` both returns a value and mutates - a method is free to do both, which is why the discarded return in line four still changes the state.

exam.prompt: Build `Ledger`, combining everything on this floor. `__init__(self, entries)` stores its **own copy** of a list of amounts; `record(amount)` appends one; `__len__` gives the number of entries; `__eq__` is true when another ledger holds the same entries in the same order; and the generator method `running_total()` yields the balance after each entry. Then write `audit(entries, extra)` which builds a `Ledger` from `entries`, records every amount in `extra`, and returns the list `[len(ledger), list(ledger.running_total()), ledger == Ledger(entries)]`.
exam.explain: The copy in `__init__` is what makes the last element of the result meaningful: alias the caller's list instead and `record` would edit `entries` too, so the freshly built comparison ledger would always match and every expected `False` would come out `True`. The running total has to be an accumulator carried across `yield` statements - the frame survives each pause, so the variable does too.
exam.hint: Keep a total variable outside the loop and yield it after each addition.

sections.title: Defaults and Named Arguments
sections.body:
A **parameter** is the name written in the `def`; an **argument** is the value handed over at the call site. Giving a parameter a default makes it optional, and passing an argument **by name** lets you skip the ones in front of it instead of retyping their defaults.

A default expression is evaluated **once**, when the `def` statement runs - not on every call. That is why `def f(x, seen=[])` shares one list between every call that omits `seen`, and why the standard fix is a default of `None` plus a fresh list built inside the body.
sections.code:
def brew(base, strength=1, sugar=0):
    return f"{base} x{strength} +{sugar}"

print(brew("tea"))
print(brew("tea", 3))
print(brew("tea", sugar=2))

def log(line, seen=None):
    if seen is None:
        seen = []
    seen.append(line)
    return seen

print(log("a"), log("b"))

annotations.text: Nothing optional was given, so strength and sugar fall back to 1 and 0.
Naming sugar skips strength without repeating its default.
None as the default, then a fresh list inside: a default of [] would be built once at def time and shared by every call.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.code:
def tag(text, prefix="[", suffix="]"):
    return prefix + text + suffix

print(tag("ok"))
print(tag("ok", suffix="!"))
checkpoint.explain: Naming suffix replaces only that one default; prefix is untouched and still contributes its bracket. Skipping a middle argument is exactly what keyword arguments buy you.

sections.title: Collecting Arguments, Handing Back Several Values
sections.body:
`*args` collects every leftover **positional** argument into a tuple, and `**kwargs` collects every leftover **keyword** argument into a dict. The star is what does the collecting - the names `args` and `kwargs` are convention, nothing more.

A parameter written after `*args` can only be passed by name, which is how you build a function that takes any number of values plus a few named options. A `return` with commas builds a tuple, so one call can hand back several values and the caller unpacks them with multiple assignment.
sections.code:
def report(label, *values, **options):
    return label, sum(values), options

name, total, opts = report("run", 3, 4, 5, unit="m", fast=True)
print(name, total, opts)
print(report("empty"))

annotations.text: values is a tuple, so sum() works on it directly; options is a dict.
Three names on the left unpack the three-item tuple the return built.
With nothing left over, args is the empty tuple and kwargs the empty dict - never an error.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `count_args(*args)` returning how many positional arguments it was given.
checkpoint.explain: Because the star packs the arguments into a tuple before the body runs, counting them is just len() - and the zero-argument call gives an empty tuple rather than a TypeError.

sections.title: Functions Are Values
sections.body:
A `def` binds a function **object** to a name, and that object can be assigned, stored in a list, or passed to another function like any other value. Writing `f` refers to the function; writing `f()` calls it - dropping the parentheses is the difference between handing over a tool and handing over what it produced.

A function that takes or returns another function is **higher-order**; `sorted(key=...)` and `max(key=...)` are the ones you meet first. A `lambda` is an expression whose value is a small unnamed function, useful exactly where inventing a name would be noise.
sections.code:
def shout(text):
    return text.upper() + "!"

def apply_to_all(func, items):
    out = []
    for item in items:
        out.append(func(item))
    return out

print(apply_to_all(shout, ["a", "b"]))
print(apply_to_all(lambda s: s * 2, ["a", "b"]))

words = ["pear", "fig", "banana"]
print(sorted(words, key=len))

annotations.text: shout is passed without parentheses - the function itself, not a result.
A lambda is the same kind of value, written inline instead of with def.
sorted calls len on every word and orders by what comes back.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.code:
def double(n):
    return n * 2

ops = [double, len]
print(ops[0](5))
print(ops[1]("hello"))
checkpoint.explain: A list of functions is an ordinary list; indexing it gives back a function, and the parentheses that follow are what actually call it. Nothing about a function stops it being stored like a number or a string.

sections.title: Calling Yourself
sections.body:
A **recursive** function calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem. Two things are non-negotiable: a **base case** that returns without recursing, and a recursive case whose argument moves strictly toward that base case.

If the base case is missing, or the argument never shrinks, every call makes another call and none ever returns - the pile of unfinished calls grows until Python gives up with a `RecursionError`. Left to itself the function never terminates; that error is a safety net, not the design. Reading recursion is easiest if you assume the inner call already works for the smaller input and only check how the results are joined.

annotations.text: The base case: it returns without calling countdown again.
n - 1 is strictly smaller, so every chain of calls reaches 0.
The base case alone answers this call - no recursion happens at all.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `sum_to(n)` returning 1 + 2 + ... + n, with `sum_to(0)` returning 0. Solve it recursively.
checkpoint.explain: The base case has to answer the smallest input outright, and n - 1 guarantees you arrive there. Notice the zero case is not a special exception bolted on - it is the case that stops everything.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.code:
def power(base, exp=2):
    return base ** exp

print(power(3))
print(power(3, 3))
guided-practice.explain: The default only applies when the caller stays silent about that parameter. One definition therefore serves two calls, which is the whole reason defaults exist.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the blanks so the last line prints <<ok>>, naming both defaults at the call site.
guided-practice.explain: A keyword argument is matched by the parameter's name, not by its position, so the order you write them in at the call site does not matter. That is what lets you override one default and leave the rest alone.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `join_words(words, sep=" ")` returning the words joined by `sep`. With no separator given it joins with a single space, and an empty list returns the empty string.
guided-practice.starterCode:
def join_words(words, sep=" "):
    pass
guided-practice.solution:
def join_words(words, sep=" "):
    return sep.join(words)
guided-practice.hint: The fallback belongs in the def line, not in an if inside the body.
guided-practice.explain: Putting the fallback in the signature documents it in the one place a reader looks, and keeps the body free of a branch that exists only to invent a value. The empty list needs no special case because joining nothing is already the empty string.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this print?
guided-practice.explain: Positional and keyword arguments land in two different containers, so a value counted by one is invisible to the other. Iterating a dict yields its keys, which is why sorted(kwargs) gives names rather than values.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `min_max(numbers)` returning two values - the smallest and the largest, in that order. The list is never empty.
guided-practice.starterCode:
def min_max(numbers):
    pass
guided-practice.solution:
def min_max(numbers):
    return min(numbers), max(numbers)
guided-practice.hint: return a, b builds a tuple - no list brackets needed.
guided-practice.explain: A comma in a return statement packs the values into one tuple, which the caller can unpack straight into two names. The single-element list is the case that proves the two answers are independent of each other rather than of the list's length.

guided-practice.prompt: Order these lines into a program that applies a function twice and prints 7.
guided-practice.explain: The parameter `func` is filled with a function value at the call, so the body can invoke it without knowing its name. The lambda is created as an argument and never bound to a name at all.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `apply_all(func, items)` returning a list holding `func(item)` for every item, in order.
guided-practice.starterCode:
def apply_all(func, items):
    pass
guided-practice.hint: func(item) - the parameter is called exactly like any other function.
guided-practice.explain: The function never learns what it is applying, which is precisely what makes one definition work for doubling, measuring and uppercasing alike. Behaviour arrives as an argument instead of being hard-coded in the body.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `factorial(n)` returning n! for n >= 0, where `factorial(0)` is 1. Solve it recursively.
guided-practice.starterCode:
def factorial(n):
    pass
guided-practice.hint: n! is n times (n-1)!, and 0! is 1.
guided-practice.explain: Returning 1 at the bottom is what makes the whole product come out right - it is the multiplicative identity, not an arbitrary choice. Each frame waits on the one below it, so nothing is actually multiplied until the base case answers.

debugging.prompt: `two_baskets('a', 'b')` should return `[['a'], ['b']]` - two separate baskets. It returns `[['a', 'b'], ['a', 'b']]` instead. Fix `add_item` without changing how it is called.
debugging.hint: How many times is the [] on the def line actually evaluated?
debugging.explain: The empty list is built once, when the def executes, so every default-using call appends into that same object and hands back the same list. A default of None is a value nobody can mutate, and the body builds a fresh list each time it sees one.

debugging.prompt: `countdown(3)` should return `[3, 2, 1]` and `countdown(0)` should return `[]`. Instead every call runs until Python raises RecursionError. Fix it.
debugging.hint: Nothing here ever returns without recursing first.
debugging.explain: n does shrink, but nothing checks whether it has arrived - so the calls sail past zero into the negatives and never stop. A base case is a guard placed before the recursive call, and it has to answer the smallest input outright.

debugging.prompt: `sum_digits(123)` should return 6. This one has a base case, yet it still never terminates. Fix it.
debugging.hint: The recursive call is handed exactly the problem it was already given.
debugging.explain: Having a base case is not enough - the argument must move toward it, and passing n unchanged means every call faces an identical problem forever. Integer division by 10 drops the digit you just consumed, which is what makes the input strictly smaller.

debugging.prompt: `tally(1, 2, 3)` should return 6 and `tally(1, 2, start=10)` should return 13, but every call with more than one number raises a TypeError. Fix the signature.
debugging.hint: One star turns a single parameter into a collector.
debugging.explain: Without the star the function has room for exactly one positional value, so a second one has nowhere to go. Adding it also makes `start` keyword-only - anything after `*counts` can no longer be reached by position, which is exactly the protection an option wants.

challenge-set.prompt: Write `profile(name, **details)` returning a dict with key `"name"` holding the name, plus one entry for every keyword argument given.
challenge-set.starterCode:
def profile(name, **details):
    pass
challenge-set.hint: details is already a dict - you only have to add the name to it.
challenge-set.explain: **details leaves the function open to fields nobody has thought of yet, without editing the signature every time one appears. The no-keyword call needs no branch because an empty dict contributes nothing.

challenge-set.prompt: Write `keep(items, test)` returning a list of the items for which `test(item)` is true, in their original order.
challenge-set.starterCode:
def keep(items, test):
    pass
challenge-set.hint: Call test(item) inside the if - do not compare it to True.
challenge-set.explain: The condition is supplied by the caller, so the traversal and the decision are cleanly separated - one is control flow you write once, the other is policy that changes per call. A lambda fits here because the test is too small to deserve a name.

challenge-set.prompt: Write `to_binary(n)` returning the binary digits of a non-negative integer as a string, with `to_binary(0)` returning `"0"`. Solve it recursively - do not use bin().
challenge-set.starterCode:
def to_binary(n):
    pass
challenge-set.hint: n % 2 is the last digit; n // 2 is everything in front of it.
challenge-set.explain: The digits fall out least-significant first, so the recursive call has to be placed to the left of the digit you just computed - the order of concatenation is the whole trick. Stopping below 2 handles 0 and 1 on the same line, because each is already its own binary form.

challenge-set.prompt: This function has a base case, yet `shrink([1, 2])` never returns a value. Explain what is wrong and what happens inside Python while it runs.
challenge-set.explain: Termination needs two independent guarantees: a case that stops, and an argument that provably approaches it. Only the first is present here, so each call adds a frame that can never be discarded, and the growing stack - not the logic - is what finally halts the program.

challenge-set.prompt: Trace `total(3)`. Give the value each call returns, innermost first.
challenge-set.explain: Nothing is added on the way down - every frame parks its n and waits. The additions all happen on the way back up, which is why the base case's value is the seed the whole sum is built on.

challenge-set.prompt: Write `run_pipeline(value, *steps, repeat=1)`. It applies every function in `steps` to `value` in order, repeats that whole chain `repeat` times, and returns the final value. With no steps, or with repeat=0, it returns the value unchanged. No starter code.

tests.input: 5, lambda n: n + 1, lambda n: n * 2

challenge-set.explain: Rebinding `value` on every step is what chains the functions together - the result of one call becomes the input of the next with no temporary names. `repeat` has to sit after *steps so that a function being passed in can never be mistaken for it.

exam.prompt: Given `def collect(x, into=[]):` whose body appends x to into and returns into - one program calls `collect(1)`, then `collect(2)`. What does the second call return?
exam.explain: The default list is created once at definition time, so both calls mutate the same object and the second sees what the first left behind. This is the classic function that looks correct in isolation and misbehaves the moment it is called twice.

exam.prompt: Given `def f(a, b=2, *rest, **opts): ...`, which of these calls are legal?
exam.explain: `a` has no default, so it must be supplied somehow - by position or by name - and the call that omits it fails before the body ever runs. Everything unclaimed falls into *rest or **opts, which is why an unexpected keyword is accepted here instead of raising.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.code:
def wrap(*args, **kwargs):
    return args, kwargs

print(wrap(1, 2))
print(wrap(a=1))
print(wrap())
exam.explain: The two containers are always present, empty or not, and the return packs them into a further tuple - which is why the printed shape is a tuple holding a tuple and a dict. Recognising `()` and `{}` as the empty forms saves you from writing a needless guard.

exam.prompt: Fill the blanks so the words are sorted by length, using an unnamed function.
exam.explain: sorted stops comparing the words themselves once a key is given - it compares what the key function returns for each of them. The lambda is an ordinary argument here, created and passed in a single expression.

exam.prompt: Order these lines into a recursive function that counts the items in a list.
exam.explain: The base case is written first because it must be tested before any recursive call is made; place it afterwards and the call happens unconditionally. Slicing off the head is what makes the argument strictly smaller each time.

exam.prompt: Trace `to_binary(6)`. Give what each call returns, innermost first.
exam.explain: Each frame contributes exactly one digit, appended to whatever the frame below it built - so the string grows left to right as the stack unwinds. Tracing the returns rather than the calls is how you check the assembly order of a recursive result.

exam.prompt: `sorted(words, key=len)` works, but `sorted(words, key=len())` fails immediately. Explain the difference the parentheses make and what sorted actually needs here.
exam.explain: A name without parentheses evaluates to the function object itself, which sorted can store and invoke once per item; with parentheses you run it immediately and hand over whatever came back. Every higher-order technique rests on that one distinction.

exam.prompt: `fib(6)` should return 8 for the sequence 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. It returns a far larger number. Fix it.
exam.hint: Which two earlier numbers make up a Fibonacci number?
exam.explain: Both halves of the sum recursed on the same subproblem, so the function doubles at every level and computes a power of two instead of the sequence - a correct base case cannot rescue a wrong recursive case. The two branches have to describe two different smaller problems.

exam.prompt: Write `config(**overrides)` returning the settings dict `{"host": "localhost", "port": 8080}` with every keyword argument applied on top of it.
exam.starterCode:
def config(**overrides):
    pass
exam.hint: Build the defaults inside the body, then write the overrides over them.
exam.explain: Building the defaults inside the body rather than in the signature sidesteps the shared-mutable-default trap entirely, because a new dict is made per call. Applying overrides afterwards means the caller never has to restate the settings they were happy with.

exam.prompt: Write `best(items, score)` returning the item with the highest `score(item)`. On a tie keep the earlier item, and return None for an empty list.
exam.starterCode:
def best(items, score):
    pass
exam.hint: Keep the best score seen so far alongside the item that earned it.
exam.explain: Comparing with a strict > is what makes a tie keep the earlier item - switching to >= silently reverses that rule. Because the ranking arrives as an argument, one function finds the longest word and the number furthest from zero without knowing either idea.

exam.prompt: Write `apply_until(value, func, stop, limit=10)`. Apply `func` to `value` again and again until `stop(value)` is true, then return two values: the final value and how many times func was applied. Never apply func more than `limit` times, even if stop never becomes true. No starter code.

tests.input: 1, lambda n: n * 2, lambda n: n > 10
5, lambda n: n + 1, lambda n: n > 3
1, lambda n: n + 1, lambda n: False, 3
'a', lambda s: s + 'a', lambda s: len(s) == 3
7, lambda n: n + 1, lambda n: False, 0

exam.explain: Two functions arrive as arguments - one that transforms and one that decides - and the count travels back up alongside the value as a tuple, so no shared state is needed. `limit` is a base case in disguise: it guarantees termination even when the caller's stop condition never becomes true.

sections.title: try, except, else, finally
sections.body:
A `try` block runs code that might fail. If it raises, Python looks for an `except` clause naming that exception's class - or a parent of it - and runs the first one that matches.

The optional `else` block runs **only** when nothing was raised, which keeps the risky line and the follow-up work visibly separate. `finally` runs no matter what: exception, no exception, even when the `try` block already hit a `return`.

Catch the **specific** class you know how to handle. A bare `except:` catches everything, including the typo you have not found yet.

annotations.text: KeyError, not Exception - this handler claims one failure and no others.
else runs only on the no-exception path, so a failure in the follow-up work is never mistaken for a lookup failure.
finally still runs even though both branches above it already returned.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this program print?
checkpoint.explain: Both calls reach the finally block: the first arrives after the try succeeded, the second after the handler ran. That is the whole point of finally - it is the one block whose execution does not depend on which path was taken.

sections.title: Building One Class on Another
sections.body:
`class RunicWard(Ward)` says a RunicWard **is a** Ward: it inherits every method Ward defines, for free.

Defining a method the parent already has **overrides** it. `super()` reaches past your override to the parent's version, so you can extend behaviour instead of retyping it.

A subclass that writes its own `__init__` must call `super().__init__(...)` itself - Python does not do it for you, and skipping it leaves every parent attribute unset.

annotations.text: Without this call, self.name and self.strength would never exist.
super().describe() runs Ward's version, then this method adds to its result.
isinstance follows the inheritance chain, which is what makes `is a` literally true.

checkpoint.prompt: `Loud` should behave exactly like `Note` except that `text()` returns the body uppercased. Override `text()` in `Loud`, building the uppercase result from the parent's version rather than from `self.body`.
checkpoint.explain: Going through super().text() means the subclass keeps working when Note later changes how it stores or formats its body. Reaching for self.body instead quietly copies the parent's implementation into the child, and copies rot.

sections.title: Raising, and Errors of Your Own
sections.body:
`raise` throws an exception yourself. It is how a function refuses a bad argument instead of returning a nonsense value that the caller will misread three frames later.

Exceptions are ordinary classes, so you make your own by subclassing `Exception` - everything from the previous section applies. A small hierarchy pays off immediately: `except WardError` also catches `WardBreached`, because a WardBreached **is a** WardError.

Give the subclass extra attributes when the handler needs data rather than prose, and pass the human-readable message up with `super().__init__(...)`.

annotations.text: WardBreached inherits from WardError, so one except clause can cover a whole family.
The message goes to Exception's own __init__; str(e) reads it back later.
A built-in class is the right choice when the failure is a plain bad argument.
The handler names the parent and still catches the child.

checkpoint.prompt: Make `descend(depth)` raise `TooDeep` with the message `too deep` when `depth` is greater than 3, and otherwise return `depth`. Then make `safe_descend(depth)` return whatever `descend` returned, or the error's message text if it raised.
checkpoint.explain: Raising and handling are two different jobs, and splitting them across two functions is what lets the same rule be enforced in one place and recovered from in many. str(e) recovers the message because Exception stored it when you passed it in.

sections.title: with, __enter__ and __exit__
sections.body:
Some objects need cleaning up: a lock released, a buffer flushed, a connection closed. Doing that by hand means every early `return` and every exception is another chance to forget.

A `with` statement makes the cleanup structural. Python calls the object's `__enter__` on the way in, binds whatever it returns to the `as` name, and **guarantees** `__exit__` on the way out - normal exit or exception, it runs.

`__exit__` receives the exception's type, value and traceback, all `None` when the block finished normally. Return a falsy value and the exception carries on outwards; return `True` and you have silently swallowed it.

annotations.text: Whatever __enter__ returns is what `as log` is bound to - usually self.
return False lets any exception continue outwards; True would swallow it.
The RuntimeError escapes the with block, but 'closed' was already appended on the way out.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this program print?
checkpoint.explain: The three arguments to __exit__ are the exception's type, value and traceback, and they are all None on the clean path - which is exactly how a context manager tells success from failure without being told.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print?
guided-practice.explain: True division always produces a float, so 9 / 3 is 3.0 and not 3. The second call never reaches the return inside try - control jumps to the handler the moment the division raises.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the blanks so this parses `raw`, falls back to 0 on bad text, reports the value only when parsing succeeded, and always prints `done`.
guided-practice.template:
raw = '12'
try:
    value = int(raw)
___ ValueError:
    value = 0
___:
    print('parsed', value)
___:
    print('done')
guided-practice.explain: Moving the success work into else instead of leaving it at the end of try means a ValueError raised by that work is no longer mistaken for a parsing failure. finally comes last because it belongs to every path rather than to one of them.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `to_int(text)` returning `int(text)`, or `0` when `text` cannot be parsed as an integer. Catch only the exception `int` actually raises for bad text.
guided-practice.starterCode:
def to_int(text):
    pass
guided-practice.explain: int('') and int('abc') both raise ValueError, so one specific handler covers both without also catching the TypeError you would get from passing a list. Screening the text yourself with isdigit() instead would wrongly reject '-7'.
guided-practice.hint: int() raises ValueError - not TypeError - when the text is not a number.

guided-practice.prompt: `Spell.describe()` returns text like `Mend (2 mana)`. Finish `Ritual` so it takes `name, cost, minutes`, reuses `Spell.__init__` for the first two, and overrides `describe()` to append ` [5 min]` to the parent's text - so `ritual_line('Mend', 2, 5)` returns `Mend (2 mana) [5 min]`.
guided-practice.explain: Two calls to super() do two different jobs here: one hands the shared attributes to the parent's initialiser, the other borrows the parent's formatting. Neither line repeats anything Spell already knows, which is the test for whether inheritance is buying you anything.
guided-practice.hint: Ritual needs its own __init__ that calls super().__init__(name, cost) first.

guided-practice.prompt: Make `cast(pool, cost)` raise `InsufficientMana` with the message `f"need {cost}, have {pool}"` when `cost` is greater than `pool`, and otherwise return the mana left over. Then make `cast_or_report(pool, cost)` return that remainder, or the error's message text when the cast is refused - so `cast_or_report(2, 5)` returns `need 5, have 2`.
guided-practice.explain: A named class is worth more than a boolean return here: a caller that cannot recover simply lets InsufficientMana travel, while one that can names it in an except clause. Note that cost == pool is allowed, which is the boundary a `>=` test would get wrong.
guided-practice.hint: Only `cost > pool` is a failure - spending your last point is legal.

guided-practice.prompt: `run_tally` is already written and uses `Tally` in a `with` block. Give `Tally` the two methods that make that legal: `__enter__` returning the tally itself, and `__exit__` setting `self.closed` to `True` without suppressing anything.
guided-practice.explain: An object is usable in a with statement purely because it has those two methods - there is no interface to register and nothing to inherit from. Returning self from __enter__ is a convention rather than a rule, but it is what makes `with Tally() as t` read the way people expect.
guided-practice.hint: __exit__ takes exactly three arguments after self: exc_type, exc_value, traceback.

debugging.prompt: `parse_ratio('6/0')` should return `infinite`, but it returns `bad input`. Both handlers are present and both are individually correct. Fix the function without changing either message.
debugging.explain: Python takes the first except clause whose class matches, and ZeroDivisionError is a subclass of Exception, so a broad clause placed above it can never be reached. Order except clauses most specific first - nothing warns you about the dead one.
debugging.hint: Which clause does Python try first, and does ZeroDivisionError match it?

debugging.prompt: `dragon_status('Vex', 40, 'fire')` should return `Vex: 40 hp (fire)` but crashes with `AttributeError: 'Dragon' object has no attribute 'name'`. Fix `Dragon` without touching `Creature`.
debugging.explain: Writing __init__ in a subclass replaces the parent's initialiser outright; nothing calls it implicitly. The attributes it would have set simply never exist, and the failure surfaces far from its cause - inside status(), which is why the traceback names the wrong method.
debugging.hint: Overriding __init__ is still overriding. What has to run before self.breath is set?

debugging.prompt: `guard(True)` should return `['open', 'close', 'error escaped']` because the ValueError escapes the `with` block, but it returns `['open', 'close', 'no error']`. Fix `Gate` without changing `guard`.
debugging.explain: A truthy return from __exit__ is Python's one way of saying `I have dealt with this exception, stop unwinding` - so returning True turns every failure inside the block into silence. Cleanup and suppression are separate decisions, and only a manager that genuinely handles the error should make the second one.
debugging.hint: The cleanup itself runs correctly. Look at what __exit__ hands back afterwards.

debugging.prompt: `attempt('iron', 'gold')` should return `refused: 'iron' does not fit`, but the WrongKey escapes `attempt` uncaught. Fix it by changing one line, and do not widen the `except` clause.
debugging.explain: `except VaultError` matches that class and its descendants, and WrongKey was declared a sibling rather than a child - so the family it appears to belong to is not the family Python sees. Rooting your errors in one base class is what lets callers pick their own granularity later without you editing every raise site.
debugging.hint: What does WrongKey inherit from now, and what would `except VaultError` need it to inherit from?

challenge-set.prompt: `run(0)` is called. Give the letters it prints, in order, one per step.
challenge-set.code:
def run(x):
    print("A")
    try:
        print("B")
        y = 10 // x
        print("C")
    except ZeroDivisionError:
        print("D")
    else:
        print("E")
    finally:
        print("F")
    print("G")

run(0)
challenge-set.explain: C is skipped because the raise abandons the rest of the try block immediately, and E is skipped because else belongs to the no-exception path only. F and G both still run: the handler dealt with the exception, so execution resumes normally after the statement.

challenge-set.prompt: A teammate replaces `with Ledger() as log:` with three plain statements: `log = Ledger().__enter__()`, then the block's code, then `log.__exit__(None, None, None)`. It passes every test they wrote. Explain what goes wrong the first time a line inside that block raises, and what the `with` statement is doing that their rewrite is not.
challenge-set.explain: The rewrite is only correct on the happy path: an exception - or an early return, or a break - jumps past the __exit__ call and the resource is never released. `with` compiles to an implicit try/finally, which is why its guarantee holds for every way of leaving the block rather than just the one the tests exercised.

challenge-set.prompt: Give `FieldError` an `__init__(self, field)` that passes the message `f"missing {field}"` up to `Exception` and stores `self.field = field`. Make `check(record)` raise it for the first of `'name'`, `'level'` missing from the dict and return `'ok'` when both are present. Then make `report(records)` return a list holding, for each record in order, either `'ok'` or the name of its first missing field.
challenge-set.explain: Carrying `field` as an attribute rather than parsing it back out of the message text is the difference between an exception a program can act on and one only a human can read. Catching inside the loop, not around it, is what lets one bad record be reported without abandoning the rest.
challenge-set.hint: e.field is available on the caught exception because __init__ put it there.

challenge-set.prompt: Nothing is given to you. Write a context manager class `Transaction` whose `__init__` sets `self.applied = []`, whose `__enter__` returns the transaction, whose `apply(item)` appends `item` to `self.applied`, and whose `__exit__` empties `self.applied` when the block is leaving because of an exception, leaves it untouched otherwise, and never suppresses the exception. Then write `run_transaction(items, fail_on)`: it applies each item in order inside a `with` block, raises `ValueError` immediately after applying an item equal to `fail_on`, catches that `ValueError` outside the `with`, and returns the transaction's `applied` list.
challenge-set.explain: The three arguments to __exit__ are not decoration: `exc_type is not None` is the entire test for `did this block fail`, and it is what turns a context manager from a cleanup hook into a rollback. Returning a falsy value keeps the two responsibilities apart - undo the work, but let the caller still learn that it failed.

challenge-set.prompt: Add `ManaError` and `TargetError` as subclasses of `SpellError`. Make `classify(kind)` raise `ManaError` for `'mana'`, `TargetError` for `'target'`, `SpellError` for `'other'`, and return `'fine'` for anything else. Then make `describe(kind)` return `'mana problem'`, `'target problem'`, `'spell problem'` or `'fine'` using a single `try` with three `except` clauses.
challenge-set.explain: The hierarchy is what gives the caller a choice of granularity: one clause for everything spell-related, or a separate clause per cause. It only works if the clauses are ordered leaf-first, because `except SpellError` would otherwise absorb both children before their own handlers were consulted.
challenge-set.hint: Put the two children above the parent in your except chain.

exam.prompt: A function hits a `return` inside its `try` block, and that `try` also has a `finally`. When does the `finally` block run?
choices: It is skipped, because return leaves the function immediately
After the return value is computed, but before the caller receives it
Only when an exception was raised
After the caller has already received the value
exam.explain: The return value is evaluated, then held while finally runs, then handed over. That ordering is exactly why a `return` inside finally overwrites it - the pending value is still in flight when the block executes.

exam.prompt: An exception is raised inside a `with` block, and the context manager's `__exit__` returns `True`. What happens next?
choices: The exception is re-raised as soon as __exit__ finishes
The exception is suppressed and execution continues after the with block
The with block runs again from the top
Python raises a TypeError because __exit__ must return None
exam.explain: A truthy return is the protocol's way of saying the manager handled the exception, so the interpreter stops unwinding. It is the one line that turns a cleanup helper into an error swallower, which is why almost every __exit__ you write should end in a falsy value.

exam.prompt: Which of these are true of `super().__init__(...)` written inside a subclass's own `__init__`?
choices: It runs the parent's initialiser, so the parent's attributes get set
Python calls it for you even if you never write it
It lets the subclass set its own attributes after the parent's are in place
It is only legal when the parent inherits directly from object
exam.explain: Defining __init__ replaces the parent's version rather than adding to it, so the call is yours to make and yours to place. Where you place it matters: parent state first, then the subclass's own, so the parent never observes a half-built object.

exam.prompt: What does this program print?
exam.explain: Each finally line appears before its returned value because the print inside the function runs while the return is still pending, and the caller's print only happens once the call has come back. The else branch runs on the first call and is skipped on the second.

exam.prompt: Fill the blanks so `Session` can be used as a context manager and the statement below actually uses it.
exam.explain: Those two dunder names are the entire contract - any object defining them works in a with statement, and no object without them does, whatever else it defines. The three extra parameters on the second one are not optional: Python always passes them.

exam.prompt: Order these fragments into a program that defines a custom exception and raises it when `n` exceeds 3.
exam.explain: The class has to exist before any line raises it, because `raise RetryLimit(n)` is looked up when the line runs, not when the function is defined. The bare `return n` sits outside the if, so it is reached only when the guard above it did not fire.

exam.prompt: A teammate wraps a 40-line function in `try: ... except Exception: return None`. It has not crashed since. Last week the team spent two days chasing a wrong total that turned out to be a misspelled dictionary key. Explain what the broad handler cost them, and what you would write instead.
exam.explain: A handler that catches everything cannot distinguish a failure it anticipated from a bug it has never seen, so the KeyError from the typo became a plausible-looking None and travelled onwards disguised as data. Naming the classes you can actually recover from keeps the ones you cannot loud, and a loud crash is far cheaper than a quiet wrong answer.

exam.prompt: `total([1, 'x'])` should return `-1` because the text cannot be converted, but it returns `1`. Fix the function so the `except` clause's value is the one that reaches the caller.
exam.explain: A `return` inside finally replaces any value already on its way out - and would equally discard an exception that was still propagating. finally is for cleanup that must happen; deciding what the function answers is not cleanup.
exam.hint: Which return actually wins when both the except clause and the finally block have one?

exam.prompt: Override `cost()` in both subclasses so each builds on the class above it: `Enchanted` doubles the parent's cost, `Cursed` subtracts 1 from the parent's cost. So `cursed_cost(10)` returns `19`.
exam.explain: Each super() call moves exactly one step up the chain, so the three implementations compose into base * 2 - 1 without any class knowing more than its immediate parent. Hard-coding `self.base * 2 - 1` in Cursed would pass these tests and break the moment Enchanted's rule changed.
exam.hint: Cursed's super() is Enchanted, not Tool.

exam.prompt: Build a small audit log. Add `Rejected` as a subclass of `AuditError`. Make `Audit` a context manager: `__enter__` returns the audit, `record(entry)` raises `Rejected(entry)` when `entry` is the empty string and otherwise appends it to `self.entries`, and `__exit__` appends the string `closed` to `self.entries` and suppresses nothing. Then make `audit(entries)` create one `Audit`, record every entry in order inside a `with` block, catch `AuditError` around that whole block, and return the audit's `entries`. So `audit(['a', '', 'c'])` returns `['a', 'closed']`.
exam.explain: Everything on this floor meets here: `closed` still appears after a rejection because __exit__ runs on the way out of a failing block, `'c'` never appears because the raise abandoned the loop, and `except AuditError` catches Rejected only because inheritance made them one family. The try has to sit outside the with, or the cleanup would land after the handler rather than before it.
exam.hint: The with block goes inside the try, so the exception leaves the block before you catch it.

sections.title: Comprehensions
sections.body:
A **comprehension** states what a collection contains instead of describing the loop that fills it. The shape is always the same: an expression, a `for` clause, and an optional `if` filter that decides which items survive.

The brackets choose the container - `[...]` builds a list, `{k: v for ...}` builds a dict, and `{...}` with a bare expression builds a set.

The loop variable lives only inside the comprehension, so it never leaks into the surrounding code the way a `for` loop's variable does.
sections.code:
nums = [3, 8, 1, 12, 7]
squares = [n * n for n in nums if n % 2 == 1]
by_value = {n: n * n for n in nums if n > 5}
parities = {n % 2 for n in nums}
print(squares)
print(by_value)
print(sorted(parities))

annotations.text: Expression, then for, then filter: only odd values reach `n * n`.
A dict comprehension needs `key: value` before the for clause.
Braces with a single expression build a set, so the duplicate parities collapse.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.code:
words = ["ash", "ember", "kiln", "ore"]
print([w.upper() for w in words if len(w) == 3])
checkpoint.explain: The filter runs before the expression, so `.upper()` is only ever applied to the words that survived it. Order is preserved because a list comprehension walks the source in order.

sections.title: The Iterator Protocol
sections.body:
A `for` loop is not magic: it calls `iter()` on whatever you gave it, then calls `next()` on the result until `StopIteration` is raised.

Any object can join in by defining two methods. `__iter__` returns the iterator - for a self-consuming object that is simply `self` - and `__next__` produces the next value or raises `StopIteration` to signal exhaustion.

The state that decides what comes next lives on the object, which is why a half-consumed iterator cannot be rewound.

annotations.text: Returning self makes the object its own iterator.
Exhaustion is signalled by raising, never by returning None.
list() drives the protocol to completion for you.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `take_two(source)` that returns a list of the first two items produced by any iterable, using `iter()` and `next()` rather than slicing.
checkpoint.explain: `iter()` is what turns a list or a string into something `next()` can drive; calling `next()` twice on the same iterator advances it, which is exactly why the second call does not hand back the first item again.

sections.title: Decorators
sections.body:
A **decorator** is a function that takes a function and returns a replacement. `@announce` above a `def` means `spark = announce(spark)` - nothing more.

The replacement usually accepts `*args, **kwargs` so it can stand in for any signature, and `functools.wraps` copies the original's name and docstring onto it so the disguise survives introspection.

A decorator that takes arguments is one layer deeper: `repeat(2)` is called first and must return the actual decorator.

Stacked decorators apply bottom-up, so the one nearest the `def` wraps first.

annotations.text: Without this line spark.__name__ would report 'wrapper'.
Three levels: the factory takes the argument, decorate takes the function, wrapper takes the call.
Applied first because it is closest to the def.
wraps is why this prints spark and not wrapper.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.explain: The name `greet` is now bound to `wrapper`, so the original function is only reachable through the closure. `functools.wraps` is what keeps the reported name honest even though the object underneath has changed.

sections.title: Type Hints
sections.body:
An **annotation** records what a value is meant to be. Since Python 3.9 the builtin containers are subscriptable directly - `list[str]`, `dict[str, int]` - with no import needed.

`Optional[str]` from `typing` means a str or None, which is the honest signature for any function that can fail to find something.

Python does not check these at runtime; it stores them in the function's `__annotations__` dict and moves on. They are for readers, editors and type checkers, not for enforcement.

annotations.text: Parameter hints go after the colon, the return hint after the arrow.
A local variable can be annotated too, even though nothing checks it.
Optional[str] documents the None-returning branch below.
The hints are just data hanging off the function object.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.code:
def double(n: int) -> int:
    return n * 2


print(double("ab"))
print(double(4))
checkpoint.explain: The annotation is a promise to the reader, not a guard at the door - `*` on a string repeats it, and Python never consults the hint. This is why a type checker is a separate tool you have to run.

unseen-challenge.prompt: Write `loud_words(words)` returning a new list containing the uppercase form of every word longer than three characters, in the original order. Build it with a single list comprehension. Nothing is given to you.
unseen-challenge.explain: Filter first, transform second - putting `.upper()` in the expression slot and the length test in the `if` slot keeps each concern in one place. The empty list falls out for free because a comprehension over nothing produces nothing; no special case is needed.
unseen-challenge.solution:
def loud_words(words):
    return [w.upper() for w in words if len(w) > 3]

unseen-challenge.prompt: Write `length_map(words)` returning a dict that maps each word to its length, skipping any empty string. Use a single dict comprehension.
unseen-challenge.explain: A dict comprehension needs `key: value` before the `for`, and an empty string is falsy so `if w` is enough to drop it. Duplicate keys are not an error - the later pair simply overwrites the earlier one, which is why two copies of the same word collapse to one entry.
unseen-challenge.solution:
def length_map(words):
    return {w: len(w) for w in words if w}

unseen-challenge.prompt: Write `unique_initials(names)` returning a sorted list of the distinct lowercase first letters of the names, ignoring any empty string. Collect the distinct letters with a set comprehension, then sort the result.
unseen-challenge.explain: A set comprehension collapses duplicates during the single pass instead of afterwards, but a set has no order you may rely on - `sorted()` is what turns it back into something a test can compare. The `if n` guard matters because indexing position 0 of an empty string raises IndexError.
unseen-challenge.solution:
def unique_initials(names):
    return sorted({n[0].lower() for n in names if n})

unseen-challenge.prompt: Write an iterator class `Countdown` whose constructor takes a start value. `__iter__` must return the object itself, and `__next__` must hand back `start`, then `start - 1`, and so on down to 1, then raise `StopIteration`. Also write `countdown_list(start)` returning `list(Countdown(start))`. The tests call `countdown_list`.
unseen-challenge.explain: `list()` only knows how to drain the object because `__iter__` handed it something with `__next__`; returning `self` is what makes the object serve as both. The stop test has to come before the value is produced, otherwise a start of 0 emits a bogus item before quitting - which is exactly what the zero and negative cases catch.

unseen-challenge.prompt: Write a decorator `doubled` that doubles whatever the wrapped function returns, preserving the wrapped function's name with `functools.wraps`. Apply it to `add(a, b)`, which returns `a + b`. Then write `probe(a, b)` returning the two-element list `[add(a, b), add.__name__]`. The tests call `probe`, so a wrapper without `functools.wraps` will fail them.
unseen-challenge.explain: After decoration the name `add` points at the wrapper, so every attribute you read from it belongs to the wrapper unless `functools.wraps` copied the original's across. That is the whole reason the second element of the list is a test and not decoration: it is the only observable difference between a wrapper that used `wraps` and one that did not.

unseen-challenge.prompt: Write a decorator factory `clamp_to(limit)`. A function it decorates returns its own result when that result is at most `limit`, and `limit` otherwise. Use `functools.wraps` on the wrapper. Apply `@clamp_to(100)` to `total(numbers: list[int]) -> int`, which returns the sum of the list, and annotate it exactly as written. The tests call `total`.
unseen-challenge.explain: A decorator that takes an argument needs three nested functions: the factory captures `limit`, the middle layer captures the function, and only the innermost one sees the call. The `[100]` case is the boundary that separates a correct `<=` from an off-by-one `<`, and the empty list proves `sum([])` is 0 rather than an error.

exam.prompt: A module runs `squares = [n * n for n in range(3)]` and nothing else. What happens if the next line evaluates `n`?
choices: It is 2, the last value the comprehension used
It is 3, one past the last value
It raises NameError - the comprehension has its own scope
exam.explain: A comprehension runs in its own implicit function scope, so its loop variable is discarded when it finishes. An ordinary `for` loop does leak its variable, and that difference is why converting a loop to a comprehension can quietly break code that read the variable afterwards.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.code:
nums = [4, 7, 2, 9]
print([n for n in nums if n > 3])
print({n: n % 3 for n in nums if n % 2 == 1})
exam.explain: Both comprehensions walk the same source in the same order, so the surviving items keep their original relative positions - a dict has kept insertion order since Python 3.7. The second filter tests the key while the stored value is a different expression entirely, which is the freedom a dict comprehension buys you.

exam.prompt: Fill the blanks so this returns the distinct lowercase initials, sorted, ignoring empty names.
exam.template:
def initials(names):
    return sorted({n[0].___() for n in names ___ n})
exam.explain: The filter clause sits after the `for`, not before it - reading a comprehension left to right gives you expression, source, condition. Normalising the case inside the comprehension is what makes the set treat 'B' and 'b' as one letter rather than two.

exam.prompt: Order these fragments into a working iterator class that counts 1 up to `limit`.
exam.explain: The exhaustion check has to run before the counter advances, otherwise the class emits one value too many. `__iter__` returning `self` is what lets the same object be both the thing you loop over and the thing that remembers where you are.

exam.prompt: Given `t = Ticker(3)` with the class below, state what each call to `next(t)` produces. For a call that does not return a value, write the name of the exception raised.
exam.explain: Each call mutates `self.i` before returning, so the iterator's position is state on the object rather than something the caller tracks. The fourth call is the important one: exhaustion is an exception, which is what a `for` loop silently catches on your behalf.

exam.prompt: Which of these statements about Python type annotations are true?
choices: `def f(xs: list[int]) -> int:` is valid on Python 3.9+ with no import
Passing a str where the hint says int raises TypeError at runtime
`Optional[str]` describes a value that is either a str or None
A function's hints can be read at runtime from its `__annotations__`
exam.explain: Hints are stored, not enforced - the interpreter records them and never looks again, which is why a mismatch is caught by a separate checker or not at all. Builtin containers became subscriptable in 3.9, so `typing.List` is now only needed for older versions.

exam.prompt: A colleague ships a decorator that does not call `functools.wraps`. Their logging output and their generated API docs are now wrong. Explain what the decorator actually did to the function, and why the fix is more than cosmetic.
exam.explain: Decoration rebinds the original name to a different object, so anything that reads attributes off that name is reading the wrapper's instead. Tooling that generates docs, logs a function name, or dispatches on identity reads exactly those attributes, which is why copying them across is a correctness fix rather than a tidiness one.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: Stacked decorators apply bottom-up but their wrappers then run top-down, so the label applied last ends up outermost in the string. The name survives two layers of wrapping because each layer used `functools.wraps`, copying the already-copied name onward.

exam.prompt: Write `char_frequency(text)` returning a dict that maps each distinct non-space character in `text` to the number of times it appears. Build the dict with a single dict comprehension over the distinct characters.
exam.explain: Iterating the distinct characters rather than the raw text is what stops the same key being recomputed once per occurrence, and a dict cannot hold a duplicate key anyway. Filtering the space inside the comprehension is cheaper and clearer than building the whole map and deleting from it afterwards.
exam.solution:
def char_frequency(text):
    return {c: text.count(c) for c in set(text) if c != " "}

exam.prompt: Write `first_over(values: list[int], limit: int) -> Optional[int]` returning the first value strictly greater than `limit`, or `None` when there is none - annotated exactly as written, with `Optional` imported from `typing`. Then write `probe(name, values, limit)` returning the two-element list `[first_over(values, limit), str(first_over.__annotations__[name])]`. The tests call `probe` and expect the annotation to stringify as `list[int]` for `values`, `<class 'int'>` for `limit`, and `typing.Optional[int]` for `return`.
exam.explain: Annotations are ordinary runtime data living in a dict keyed by parameter name, with the return hint stored under the key `return` - and what is stored is the object you wrote, not a string. That is why `int` stringifies as `<class 'int'>` while `list[int]` and `Optional[int]` print prettily: the first is the bare class, the others are typing objects with a repr designed to be read. The two None cases are what justify `Optional` in the signature - an empty source and a source where nothing clears the bar are different situations with the same honest answer.

exam.prompt: Build the whole pipeline. Write an iterator class `Chunks(values, size)` whose `__next__` returns consecutive slices of `size` items as lists and raises `StopIteration` as soon as fewer than `size` items remain. Write a decorator `sorted_result` that uses `functools.wraps` and sorts the list its wrapped function returns. Apply it to `chunk_sums(values: list[int], size: int) -> list[int]`, annotated exactly as written, which uses a comprehension over `Chunks(values, size)` to produce the sum of each full chunk. The tests call `chunk_sums`.
exam.explain: The comprehension can say `for chunk in Chunks(...)` only because the class implements the protocol - the four ideas on this floor compose rather than merely coexist. Dropping the trailing partial chunk is a decision the stop test encodes, and the decorator makes the output order deterministic without `chunk_sums` knowing anything about sorting.

sections.title: Argv Is a List of Strings
sections.body:
A command-line program is handed its arguments as **a plain list of strings** - no types, no structure, no help. By convention the first string names the command and everything after it belongs to that command, so parsing means deciding what shape each command's arguments take.

Turning that list into a **dict** such as `{"command": "add", "title": "Buy milk"}` splits reading the arguments away from doing the work, and a dict is trivial to test without ever opening a terminal.

This floor's brief is adapted from the build-your-own-x collection (codecrafters-io/build-your-own-x, CC0), which gathers specifications for rebuilding real tools from scratch.

annotations.text: Guard the empty list before indexing it - a bare argv[0] is the first crash every CLI has.
Joining the rest is what makes `greet Ada Lovelace` work: the shell split on spaces, so you put them back.
The conversion happens once, here in the parser, so the rest of the program receives a real int.
An unrecognised command is data, not an exception - the caller decides how to complain about it.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `command_name(argv)` returning the first string in `argv`, or `"help"` when `argv` is empty.
checkpoint.explain: Every argument parser opens with this guard. An empty argv is not an error case, it is what a bare command with no arguments looks like, so it deserves a defined answer rather than an IndexError.

sections.title: One Record Per Line
sections.body:
Persistence is serialisation plus a file, and the serialisation is the hard half. A **line-oriented** format - one record per line, fields joined by a separator - is readable, diffable and appendable, which is why so many real tools still use one.

`split(sep, maxsplit)` is what makes the last field safe: with a maxsplit the remainder keeps its own separators, so a note or a title containing the separator survives the trip.

Two habits prevent most bugs here - skip blank lines when reading, and never write a field you cannot read back.

annotations.text: One line per record, with the fields pasted together in a fixed order.
Skipping blank lines is what makes a trailing newline in the file harmless.
maxsplit 2 means only the first two bars are separators; the note keeps its own.
The round trip is the check that the two halves still agree with each other.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this print?
checkpoint.explain: The third line is the one that bites. Splitting the empty string does not give an empty list, it gives a list holding one empty string, so a reader that forgets to skip blank lines will try to unpack a record nobody ever wrote.

sections.title: The Round Trip Is the Test
sections.body:
A storage format is correct when `parse(serialise(x)) == x` for every `x` you care about, the empty one included. That single equality is worth more than any amount of staring at the file, because it fails loudly the moment the two halves drift apart.

Text has **no types**. Everything you write comes back as a string, so restoring the int that the serialiser flattened is the parser's job and nobody else's.

The example below shows the failure in miniature: `7` goes out, `"7"` comes back, and the round trip is broken even though the file looks perfect.

annotations.text: Writing is the easy half - the format string turns every value into text for you.
Reading is where the information was lost: value is a string here, always.
So this prints False. The file is fine; the parser is the incomplete half.
Check the empty case first - it is the one nobody ever tries by hand.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `read_scores(text)` turning lines shaped `name=score` into a dict mapping each name to its score **as an int**. Blank lines are ignored, and empty text gives `{}`.
checkpoint.explain: This is the reading half of a round trip in ten lines. The int() call is the whole point: without it the dict looks right when printed and still compares unequal to what you saved, which is the most confusing class of persistence bug there is.

trial.prompt:
**The Trial.** Build the task manager as seven functions. The acceptance tests below are the whole specification: nothing else is graded, and nothing is hidden from you.

A task is a dict `{"id": <int>, "title": <str>, "done": <bool>}`, and a task list is a list of tasks in id order.

- `parse_args(argv)` takes a list of strings with no program name. `[]` and `["list"]` both give `{"command": "list"}`. `["save"]` gives `{"command": "save"}`. `["add", "Buy", "milk"]` gives `{"command": "add", "title": "Buy milk"}`, the words joined by single spaces. `["done", "2"]` gives `{"command": "done", "id": 2}` with the id as an int. Anything else gives `{"command": "unknown", "name": argv[0]}`.
- `add_task(tasks, title)` returns a new task list with one task appended: `done` is False, and `id` is one higher than the largest id present, or 1 when the list is empty.
- `complete_task(tasks, task_id)` returns a new task list in which the task carrying that id has `done` True. An id that is not present changes nothing.
- `format_task_list(tasks)` returns `"No tasks."` for an empty list, otherwise one line per task joined by newlines, shaped `"[ ] 1 Buy milk"` and `"[x] 2 Walk dog"`.
- `serialise(tasks)` returns the file text: one line per task, `"<id>|open|<title>"` or `"<id>|done|<title>"`, joined by newlines. The empty list gives `""`.
- `parse(text)` is the exact inverse: blank lines are skipped, the id comes back as an int, and a title is allowed to contain `|`.
- `run(tasks, command)` takes a task list and one dict from `parse_args`, and returns the pair `(new_tasks, output)`.

`run` is the dispatcher, and it decides everything the user sees:

- `add` returns `(updated_tasks, "Added task 3: Buy milk")`, naming the new task's id and title.
- `done` returns `(updated_tasks, "Completed task 1: Buy milk")`, or `(tasks, "No task with id 9")` when nothing carries that id.
- `list` returns `(tasks, format_task_list(tasks))`.
- `save` returns `(tasks, serialise(tasks))`. The acceptance harness has no filesystem, so `save` hands back the exact text your program would write to `tasks.txt` rather than writing it.
- `unknown` returns `(tasks, "Unknown command: frobnicate")`.

A tuple and a two-element list are both accepted for the pair. Return new lists rather than editing the one you were handed: the real CLI reads its file once, changes the list in memory, and writes the whole thing back.
trial.explain: The dispatcher is the design. `run` knows only which small function owns each command, so every rule has exactly one home and changing the on-screen format never touches the storage format. Two details decide whether this survives real use: ids come from the largest id present rather than the length of the list, so deleting a task later cannot hand out a duplicate, and splitting with maxsplit 2 keeps a title containing a bar intact where a plain split silently corrupts it. The empty case is answered three different ways on purpose - an empty string from serialise, an empty list from parse, and "No tasks." from the formatter - because a file, a program and a human each need a different kind of nothing.
